docs.title: microlith: the macro service
docs.text:
A macro service: one team's modular Spring Boot service, with module boundaries the build enforces, deployable as one unit or as several by configuration, and a way to measure what each choice costs.

Most systems pick their shape early: a monolith that is hard to split later, or microservices with their full operational cost from day one. microlith keeps that decision open. It is not a "big monolith": a macro service is one team's bounded context, split into enforced modules, and a company is many of them connected by published contracts (principles). The code is organised as modules with strict boundaries; whether two modules share a process or talk over the network is a deployment setting, not a code change. It ships with a small order-fulfilment domain and the scripts to run it in eight shapes on one machine, so the trade-offs can be seen and measured instead of argued about.

docs.title: What it demonstrates
docs.text:
• One codebase, many shapes

    The same modules run as a single process, as three groups, or as eight services. The module code and the API interfaces never change. The eight modes

  • A single way for modules to talk

    A module reaches another only through its @RpcApi interface: a direct call in the same process, JSON-RPC 2.0 when split. No shared tables, no shared state, no hidden channels. Architecture

  • Boundaries enforced by the build

    Maven rules, ArchUnit and Spring Modulith verification fail the build when a module reaches into another. Each module owns a database schema, with separate migration and runtime roles.

  • Real measurements

    A load driver reports client round trips and the latency of every module-to-module call, per mode, with and without a result cache, parallel calls and two follow-up delivery mechanisms. Performance

docs.text:
In one processSplit across processes

  end

    O[orders]

The call pricing.quote(...) reads the same in both cases. Setting modules.pricing.enabled=false and modules.pricing.url=… in the orders process turns the method call into an HTTP request; nothing in the module code changes. It is a setting per module, so any grouping is possible.

docs.title: The demo domain
docs.text: An order-fulfilment system of eight modules (catalog, customers, pricing, inventory, payments, shipping, notifications, orders). orders.placeOrder is a saga with compensation: it validates, prices, reserves stock, authorizes payment, ships and captures; a declined payment releases the reservation, a shipping failure voids the payment and releases the reservation, and the confirmation message goes out through a durable follow-up so that a notifications outage never fails the order. A one-line order makes 17 module-to-module calls (about 20 on average in the benchmark, which uses 1 to 4 lines), with fan-out, three-deep chains and diamonds, which makes it a useful stand-in for real inter-service chatter.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
If you want to... Read Understand how it is built Architecture See the argument for not starting with microservices The case Decide how to start, where to draw boundaries and what to deploy Principles See what each of the eight shapes is, and when you would pick it Deployment modes See what the shapes cost Performance summary Run it yourself Running it Look up a term Glossary Read the original design Design document

Which code this site describes

Everything described here is on main: the eight modes, the @RpcApi model, persistence, the saga, the load driver, the @Cached result cache, parallel quotes and the switchable follow-up delivery (outbox or Spring Modulith events). The branches discuss/spring-modulith-async, spike/spring-modulith-events and spike/switchable-async, where the last two features were developed, are merged; the design notes keep their history.

Stack

Java 25, Spring Boot 4.1, Spring Modulith 2.1, PostgreSQL, Maven. Everything runs on localhost with PostgreSQL in Docker.

docs.title: Developer guide
docs.text:
How to run each deployment shape, add a module, change an API and add a service app. Design background: design/macro-service.md (section 17 lists where the code differs from it). Short overview: the root README.md.

You need a JDK 25, Docker, curl and python3. Maven comes from ./mvnw.

docs.title: 1. Run each shape locally
docs.text:
Every shape is the same code; only configuration differs. scripts/demo.sh wraps the commands below (it writes PID files and logs under .demo/).

scripts/db.sh up                        # PostgreSQL A 5432, B 5433, C 5434, schemas and roles from docs/db/bootstrap.sql
scripts/demo.sh <mode> start              # start the processes of a mode
scripts/smoke.sh                        # scenarios + expected binding on every edge + merged call tree
scripts/trace.sh <correlationId>        # the call tree of one order across all processes
scripts/demo.sh <mode> stop
scripts/db.sh down                      # stops and wipes the databases
scripts/demo-all.sh                     # every mode on a clean database, summary table
Shape <mode> Processes Cross-module calls Modulith (one jar, only the modules' -impl) modulith app-modulith :9181 all local, direct Macro service, all modules local macro-modulith app-macro profile monolith :9181 all local Macro service in groups groups app-macro profiles front :9181, fulfilment :9182, accounts :9183 local inside a group, JSON-RPC across Microservices (eight jars) microservices the eight app-<module>-service :9181-9188 all JSON-RPC Microservices from the macro jar microservices-macro app-macro eight times, profile = module name all JSON-RPC Everything through the JSON codec loopback-codec app-macro :9181 in-process, serialized Everything over HTTP to itself loopback-http app-macro :9181 HTTP to 127.0.0.1 Groups on three databases split-dbs as groups; front on A, fulfilment on B, accounts on C as groups

Without the scripts, for example the groups shape (databases up first):

./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
for g in front fulfilment accounts; do
  java -jar apps/app-macro/target/app-macro-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.profiles.active=demo,$g &
done

Changing a module's place is configuration only: modules.<m>.enabled=true|false, modules.<m>.url=http://host:port/rpc/<m> for a module that runs elsewhere, modules.<m>.binding=local|loopback-codec|loopback-http|remote to force one, modules.<m>.datasource.* for its database. Environment variables work too, for example MODULES_INVENTORY_ENABLED=false MODULES_INVENTORY_URL=http://host:9184/rpc/inventory.

Useful while running (demo profile, which implies dev): GET /demo/topology, GET /demo/trace?correlationId=, POST /demo/faults, /swagger-ui, /rpc/openapi.json, /actuator/health.

docs.title: 2. Build and test
docs.text:
./mvnw -q verify                                 # everything: boundary rules, ArchUnit, Modulith verify, contract tests, failure tests
./mvnw -q verify -pl modules/orders/orders-impl -am
scripts/check-boundaries.sh                      # forbidden dependencies must break the build
scripts/check-api-compat.sh                      # the API compatibility check must bite
scripts/new-service-app.sh --check               # generated service apps are up to date

verify writes the generated documents to apps/app-macro/target/api-docs/ and the Modulith canvases and PlantUML component diagrams to docs/generated/ (git-ignored; publish them from CI).

docs.title: 3. Add a module
docs.text:
Example: a module loyalty. Use inventory as the template.

  1. Layout. modules/loyalty/loyalty-api and modules/loyalty/loyalty-impl; list both in the root pom.xml under <modules> and <dependencyManagement>.
  2. -api (package com.acme.loyalty.api): depends only on rpc-api and other -api jars (spring-modulith-api and swagger-annotations-jakarta at provided). Contents:
  3. an interface annotated @RpcApi("loyalty"); no overloaded names; mark reads and request-id-keyed mutations @Idempotent;
  4. immutable records for parameters and results; enums, List, Map<String,…> and scalars are fine;
  5. business exceptions as unchecked classes annotated @RpcError(code = …) with a (String message) constructor and a code unique across modules;
  6. a package-info.java with @NamedInterface("api");
  7. optional @Operation(summary = …), @Parameter(description = …) and @Schema(description = …) for the generated documents.
  8. -impl (package com.acme.loyalty): depends on -api, module-support, and only the -api jars of modules it calls. Never another -impl (enforced).
  9. package-info.java: @ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = {"customers::api"}) lists what it may call; this is the single source of truth, also read by the service-app generator.
  10. Stereotypes from module-support: @ModuleService(module = "loyalty") on the class implementing the API, @ModuleComponent and @ModuleConfiguration for the rest. They make the bean conditional on modules.loyalty.enabled. Keep everything else in internal.
  11. Persistence: copy InventoryPersistenceConfiguration (own DataSource, Flyway, EntityManagerFactory, loyaltyTm; no @Primary) and annotate service methods @Transactional("loyaltyTm").
  12. Migrations: src/main/resources/db/migration/loyalty/V1__init.sql. Demo seed data, if any, goes in db/demo/loyalty/.
  13. Calling another module: inject its -api interface through the constructor.
  14. Database. Add the schema and the two roles (loyalty_migrator, DDL; loyalty_app, DML only) to docs/db/bootstrap.sql, following the existing blocks. The connection budget is per module, modules.loyalty.datasource.max-pool-size (default 3); keep the sum within the database's max_connections (design 9.1). There is no pooler.
  15. Configuration. In apps/app-macro/src/main/resources/application.yml add modules.loyalty.datasource.* (url, username, password, migration-username, migration-password); add application-loyalty.yml (the one-module profile with all other modules disabled and their URLs, copy application-inventory.yml); add the module to its group profiles (front, fulfilment, accounts, split-dbs) either enabled or with a URL; every disabled module needs a URL in every profile. Add loyalty-impl to app-modulith and app-macro.
  16. Startup validation is automatic: an enabled module without a datasource, a disabled one without a URL, a local binding without an implementation, or a loopback binding in a prod profile stops the application with a message naming the module and the property. Add a test in the style of ConnectionBehaviourTests if you add a new rule.
  17. Grouping. Decide which group (front, fulfilment, accounts) it joins in scripts/demo_tools.py (GROUPS) and in the group profiles; put its port in scripts/demo.sh and scripts/new-service-app.sh.
  18. Service app. scripts/new-service-app.sh loyalty (see section 5).
  19. Ownership and checks. A line in .github/CODEOWNERS; ./mvnw -q verify; scripts/check-boundaries.sh.

The shared ArchUnit rules (AbstractModuleArchitectureTests, from the module-support test-jar) already apply to every app and fail on a stereotype, a dependency or a cross-module use of anything but an @RpcApi type that breaks the rules.

docs.title: 4. Change an @RpcApi interface safely
docs.text:
During a rolling deployment the new version calls the old one, and the reverse, so every -api change must be additive until all deployed versions have moved on.

Change Safe? How New method yes Add it; callers of old versions never use it. A caller that already uses it fails with "method not found" against an old callee, so deploy the callee first. New field in a result record yes for JSON Keep the old constructor and delegate to the new one: public Order(a, b) { this(a, b, null); }. Old clients ignore unknown fields. New field in a parameter record careful An old caller omits it, so the callee must accept null. Remove or rename a method, parameter type, record component, exception no Deprecate first, remove a release later. japicmp fails the build. Rename a method parameter no, not detected It renames the JSON field. japicmp cannot see it; review the diff of the generated OpenRPC document. New exception yes @RpcError with a new unused code. Change an exception's code no Clients match type and code.

Procedure: change the interface, run ./mvnw -q verify (contract tests run against all four bindings), then ./mvnw verify -Dapi.compat.skip=false -Dapi.baseline.version=<last release> before merging. Keep new mutating methods idempotent through a caller-supplied request id, and annotate them @Idempotent only if repeating is safe. Mind that a local call and a remote call differ in two ways the platform already equalizes: parameters are copied (use records) and the caller's transaction is suspended (modules.boundary.suspend-transactions).

docs.title: 5. Add a deployable service app
docs.text:
A service app is a thin Spring Boot jar for one module: its -impl, exactly the -api jars it may call, and the platform.

scripts/new-service-app.sh loyalty      # one module; --all for all; --check fails if a generated app is stale

It generates apps/app-loyalty-service (pom, Application, application.yml, ApplicationTests, ArchitectureTests) from one template. The -api set comes from the module's package-info.java, and the generated pom carries a maven-enforcer rule that rejects anything else. Then add the new app to the root <modules> and <dependencyManagement> and to ensure_built in scripts/_common.sh. Do not edit a generated app by hand; change the template in scripts/new-service-app.sh and regenerate, so that all apps stay uniform.

Running a service app needs the URLs of the modules it calls (modules.<callee>.url), which the generated application.yml sets for the local demo ports.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Startup fails with "Module 'x' is disabled but modules.x.url is not set" Every @RpcApi on the classpath needs either a local implementation or a URL. RpcUnavailableException The callee is down, timed out (modules.<m>.client.read-timeout, default 10 s; connect-timeout 2 s) or its bulkhead rejected the call. Warning about the connection budget at startup The pool sizes of the enabled modules exceed platform.db.connection-budget; lower max-pool-size or raise the budget. With platform.db.enforce-budget=true startup fails instead. A bean of an @RpcApi cannot be injected by its class Local implementations are wrapped in a proxy; inject the interface. Port already in use after a crash scripts/demo.sh <mode> stop; logs are in .demo/logs/.

docs.title: Modules and assemblies
docs.text:
Every module is two Maven artifacts: <module>-api (the @RpcApi interface and its data types) and <module>-impl (the implementation). A module may depend only on the -api artifacts of the modules it calls. Applications are assemblies: they pick which -impl jars to include and which modules to enable.

graph TD
  subgraph apps
    M[app-modulith<br/>every impl, fixed all-local]
    X[app-macro<br/>every impl, profiles decide the shape]
    S["app-<module>-service ×8<br/>one impl each"]
  end
  subgraph modules
    O[orders-impl] --> OA[orders-api]
    O --> PA[pricing-api]
    P[pricing-impl] --> PA
    P --> CA[catalog-api]
  end
  subgraph platform
    R[rpc-api · rpc-spring-boot-starter]
    MS[module-support]
    D[demo-support]
  end
  apps --> modules
  modules --> platform
Part What it is platform/rpc-api @RpcApi, @Idempotent, @Cached, the Parallel helper, the exception hierarchy. No Spring dependency. platform/rpc-spring-boot-starter Server dispatch (/rpc/<module>), client proxies, transports, the boundary interceptor, the result cache layer. platform/module-support @ModuleService/@ModuleComponent/@ModuleConfiguration (a bean exists only if its module is enabled), per-module datasource, JPA and Flyway. platform/demo-support Demo profile only: topology, call tracing, fault switches, the shop page. platform/rpc-docs OpenAPI 3.1 and OpenRPC documents generated from the interfaces.

docs.title: One interface, four bindings
docs.text:
A caller injects PricingApi. What it receives depends on the module's binding:

Binding The caller gets Cost local the implementation bean itself a method call loopback-codec a proxy that serialises the call to JSON-RPC and dispatches it in the same process encoding and decoding loopback-http a proxy that sends it over HTTP to the same process a real HTTP round trip remote a proxy that sends it to the URL configured for that module network

The default is local when the implementation is present and enabled, remote otherwise. Configuration is just:

modules:
  pricing:
    enabled: false                       # not in this process
    url: http://pricing-host:9183/rpc/pricing

JSON-RPC 2.0 is served at /rpc/<module>; a convenience alias (/rpc/<module>/<method> with bare params) exists for curl. Business exceptions marked @RpcError(code = …) cross the wire and are rebuilt as the same exception class on the caller's side, so error handling is identical in every binding.

docs.title: The boundary is enforced, not conventional
docs.text:
• Maven enforcer rejects a module that depends on anything other than its allowed -api artifacts, and an app whose declared APIs do not match its module.
  • ArchUnit rules reject plain @Component/@Service/@Configuration in module packages and cross-module event use.
  • Spring Modulith verification rejects module cycles and illegal access.
  • Database roles: every module has a migration role that owns its schema and a runtime role with DML only on that schema. A module's role cannot read another module's tables, even when all eight run in one process.

docs.title: Persistence: a schema and a connection pool per module
docs.text: Each module configures its own datasource (modules.<m>.datasource.*), JPA EntityManagerFactory, transaction manager and Flyway migrations, in the PostgreSQL schema named after the module. Pools never open a connection at start-up, so an unreachable database does not stop a process, and a module that is idle holds no connection. In the split-dbs mode the groups use three PostgreSQL instances instead of one.

docs.title: orders.placeOrder: an explicit saga
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as caller
  participant O as orders
  participant X as customers / pricing / shipping
  participant I as inventory
  participant P as payments
  participant S as shipping
  C->>O: placeOrder(requestId, customer, lines)
  par independent reads
    O->>X: getCustomer
    O->>X: pricing.quote
    O->>X: shipping.quote
  end
  O->>I: reserve
  O->>P: authorize
  alt declined
    O-->>O: REJECTED + follow-up: release reservation
  else
    O->>S: createShipment
    alt shipping fails
      O-->>O: FAILED + follow-ups: void payment, release reservation
    else
      O->>P: capture
      O-->>O: CONFIRMED + follow-up: notify customer
    end
  end
  • Every step is idempotent through a request id derived from the order's (<requestId>:reserve, :authorize, :ship, :capture), and the order's persisted state (PENDING → RESERVED → AUTHORIZED → CONFIRMED, or REJECTED / FAILED) tells a repeated request where to resume.
  • Compensations and the confirmation message are follow-ups: made durable in the same transaction as the state change, delivered after the commit, retried until they succeed. See follow-up delivery.
  • There is no cross-module transaction. All ordering is explicit in orders.

docs.title: Seeing what happened
docs.text:
Aid What it shows GET /demo/topology the modules in that process, their bindings, target URLs, datasource schema GET /demo/trace?correlationId=… and scripts/trace.sh every module-to-module call of one order across all processes: caller, callee, method, binding actually used, duration, outcome, depth POST /demo/faults turn a module's failure on or off (notifications down, payments decline, inventory latency) /swagger-ui, /rpc/<module>/openapi.json generated API documentation /shop a small web page that drives the demo

The call trace is also what the performance tooling reads to attribute latency to individual calls.

docs.title: Parity risks, and how they are contained
docs.text: A local call and a remote call differ in ways that can hide bugs: a local call can share a transaction and mutable objects, a remote one cannot. The boundary interceptor makes the local path behave like the remote one where it matters (a caller's transaction is suspended around a call, calls are observed with the same tags), the same smoke scenarios run in every mode and must give identical results, and a contract test runs the same scenarios through every binding. The design document lists the remaining differences in section 11.

docs.title: Why microservices should not be the default starting point
docs.text:
Who wants their applications to go slower?

Every boundary between processes puts a network hop on every call that crosses it. In this project's measurements, splitting the same application into eight services made an order take about 2.8 times as long and cut the throughput by about two thirds (34.2 ms against 96.9 to 98.4 ms median, and 445 against 156 to 159 orders per second, 16 clients). Nobody sets out to do that, yet it is what starting with microservices does by default, before any need for the split has been shown.

Evidence, and the extrapolation from it

The numbers on this page come from this project: one domain, one machine. Carrying them over to real systems is the author's judgement, which is why the argument below is made in steps, with its limits stated at the end. In particular, every network call here was local (loopback on one machine) with no TLS, no authentication, no proxy, load balancer or service mesh in the path, so the network cost measured is a floor, not a typical figure.

Thesis. Starting a product as a set of microservices should not be the default. The default should be a macro service: one team's modular service with build-enforced module boundaries, deployed as one unit. It is the safe starting point because it keeps every later option open: the same artifact can be deployed as independent, separately scaled services without splitting the codebase and without creating separate deployables, and splitting later is far easier than merging back. Microservices-first needs an analysis that supports it. It is a decision, not a starting position.

This page argues that from the measurements and the design in this project. It is an argument from evidence, not a mathematical proof, and the last sections say where it stops.

docs.title: 1. The start is made when you know the least
docs.text: At the beginning of a product the boundaries, the volumes and the change patterns are guesses. Teams that begin with "how many services do we need?" commit to the decomposition at the point of maximum ignorance, and the usual first answer, n layers with m services per layer, is the worst one: a technical cut makes every feature a coordinated change across services. As an extrapolation from the measured cost per hop (a lower bound on one machine), the demo's 20 calls per order, each routed through two extra layer services, would be about 60 hops, roughly +70 ms, against about +10 ms for the business-aligned split. Good boundaries come from journeys, invariants and change patterns, and those appear as the product is built. See start small and let boundaries appear.

docs.title: 2. Splitting early has an immediate, measured cost
docs.text:
Same code, same tests, same workload, eight deployment shapes (the measurements). The chart and the table are means over 5 runs per mode with 16 clients (headline numbers); the call counts are from one of those runs:

Throughput by modeorders per second, 16 clients, result cache on, mean of 5 runs; larger is better0100200300400500modulith: orders/s 445 orders/smodulithorders/s: 445 orders/s445macro-modulith: orders/s 442 orders/smacro-modulithorders/s: 442 orders/s442loopback-codec: orders/s 434 orders/sloopback-codecorders/s: 434 orders/s434loopback-http: orders/s 312 orders/sloopback-httporders/s: 312 orders/s312groups: orders/s 247 orders/sgroupsorders/s: 247 orders/s247split-dbs: orders/s 250 orders/ssplit-dbsorders/s: 250 orders/s250microservices: orders/s 159 orders/smicroservicesorders/s: 159 orders/s159microservices-macro: orders/s 156 orders/smicroservices-macroorders/s: 156 orders/s156Show the numbersorders/s (orders/s)modulith445macro-modulith442loopback-codec434loopback-http312groups247split-dbs250microservices159microservices-macro156 One unit (modulith) Three groups Eight services Throughput 445 orders/s 247 (56%) 156 to 159 (35 to 36%) Median order (16 clients) 34.2 ms 62.2 ms 96.9 to 98.4 ms Remote calls per order 0 8.4 14.2 Version-skew pairs to keep compatible 0 3 13 Processes to run, patch and be on call for 1 3 8

Each call between processes costs about 1.0 to 1.7 ms more than a local one (about 0.5 ms), and an order makes about 20 calls. Cache and parallel reads win part of it back (+5 to 18% and +4 to 16% in the split modes), but those are mitigations of a cost the team chose to take on. The figures above use one shared PostgreSQL instance; giving each unit its own instance made no measurable difference (see where the evidence stops). For a single team that coordinates perfectly well, the benefit side of that bargain is mostly options it does not yet need.

docs.title: 3. Microservices mainly buy team independence; one team has no use for it yet
docs.text:
The benefits of separate services are independent deployment, scaling, failure isolation and ownership. Each is a force with evidence to gather: a cadence conflict, a measured hot spot, a differing criticality, an audit boundary, a second team. A team of 5 to 10 that releases together has none of these on day one. What it does have is the design discipline of microservices (clear contracts, ownership, data ownership, one-way dependencies), and the macro service provides that logically and enforced by the build, without running a distributed system.

The failure mode of starting with services is also a team-coordination one: a team that keeps adding services for each feature accumulates pipelines, on-call surface, patching and skew faster than its domain grows, and ends with a distributed monolith owned by one team. One team means one deployable until a force says otherwise.

docs.title: 4. The decision is asymmetric: splitting is cheap later, merging is not
docs.text:
Splitting later Merging later Deployment level configuration: enabled=false plus a URL configuration: enable it locally Contract write an API at a cut you now understand remove it and inline every consumer Data already isolated per module (no cross-schema keys, separate roles); a schema move is a metadata change, an instance move a copy collisions: each schema has its own migration history and table names Ownership one team becomes two two owners must become one A wrong boundary costs a refactor in the IDE and one commit a migration across repos, contracts and consumers

Starting in the cheap-to-be-wrong shape and moving to services on evidence loses almost nothing. Starting with services and discovering the boundaries were wrong costs a migration. See changing a boundary later.

docs.title: 5. The macro service already deploys as independent services
docs.text:
The usual objection to "start with a monolith" is that you then have to rewrite it. Here you do not. The same artifact, with different configuration, runs as one unit, as three groups, or as eight independent processes, each of which can be scaled, restarted and failed on its own:

  • microservices-macro runs the single macro jar eight times, one module enabled in each. It measured the same as the eight dedicated per-service jars (156 against 159 orders/s, within noise). So independent deployments need no separate codebase and no separate artifact.
  • The identical scenarios pass in all eight modes with identical results and exception types, and a failure suite runs eight processes while connections are cut and processes restarted.
  • Different deployments can run different versions of the artifact (a service on 1.4 while the rest are on 1.5), as long as the @RpcApi changes stay additive. japicmp enforces that once you name a baseline release.
  • Identical pods behind a router give per-API scaling and canarying with no network hop between modules, see routing.
  • Whether it still holds is a test, not a claim: the contract tests run the same scenarios through every binding, including loopback-codec (98% of the single-process throughput), on every build, and they pass only if no module relies on shared objects or a shared transaction.

What it does not give is real isolation between modules in one process, or a different runtime per module. Those are physical forces, handled by splitting that module or group when the evidence shows up.

docs.title: 6. So analyse first, and the analysis is cheap
docs.text: The default is the macro service as one unit. Deviate, per module and with a recorded reason, when a force has evidence. The forces table and the boundary-cost numbers turn "should we split this?" into a measurement: the calls per order that would cross the boundary times about 1.2 ms, against what the split buys. The cheapest extractions (notifications, payments, and read-only reference data behind a cache) are visible in the data, and the expensive ones (shipping with inventory) are visible too.

docs.title: What each starting point commits you to
docs.text: Microservices first Macro service, deployed as one unit Boundary decisions all at once, with the least information made as seams appear If a boundary is wrong a cross-service migration a refactor Runtime cost on day one about 2.8× the median latency, about a third of the throughput (this domain) baseline Operational surface N pipelines, N on-call surfaces one Version skew grows with the edges none inside the unit Can it become independent services? it already is yes, by configuration, from the same artifact Can it go back? hard (merge) trivially (enable locally) Analysis needed the one that justifies it (often skipped) the one that justifies leaving the default

docs.title: Decision record
docs.text:
Keep the choice explicit, one page per macro service:

Scope:        one bounded context, one owning team
Start:        macro service, deployed as one unit (default)
Deviations:   <module or group> -> <separate deployable>
              because <force: cadence | scale | isolation | security | tech | ownership>
              evidence: <measurement, SLO, audit finding, second team>
              cost: <crossing calls per order x ~1.2 ms>, <operational surface added>
Triggers:     what would make us split another module, and what would make us merge two
Review:       every <n> sprints, with the boundary metrics

docs.title: What the best counter-arguments say, and the answer
docs.text: Objection Answer "Our boundaries are already known and stable." Then the first split is cheap and justified. Record it as a deviation with its evidence. The default still costs nothing to start from. "We have several teams from day one." Give each team its own macro service with published contracts. The unit is the team, not the module (see many teams). "Hard isolation is required from the start (compliance, a vendor, another runtime)." Split exactly that module or group, and leave the rest together. "We have a mature platform, so a service costs little." The operational part may be cheap. The latency, throughput and version-skew costs remain, and the boundary risk is unchanged. "Real services do real work, so the hop is small by comparison." True, and it makes the relative cost smaller than measured here. A real network, TLS, authentication and any proxies make the absolute cost larger than the loopback figures. The effects point in opposite directions, so measure your own journeys. "A modular monolith erodes into a big ball of mud." It does when the boundaries are conventions. Here the build enforces them (no cross-module tables, an acyclic graph, compatibility-checked APIs) and the contract tests exercise them through every binding. "It is harder to hire or scale a team on one codebase." That is the exit ramp: a second team or a diverging vocabulary means a second macro service.

docs.title: What would change the conclusion
docs.text:
• Measured boundary cost that is negligible for your real journeys (few crossing calls per user action) and a force with evidence. Then split.
  • A domain where boundaries and volumes are genuinely known up front.
  • An organisation where independent release cadence per component is the product requirement, not a hope.

docs.title: Where the evidence stops
docs.text:
• One machine, loopback only, and nothing else in the path. Every call between processes ran over the loopback interface of one host. There was no TLS or mTLS (no handshakes, no per-call encryption), no authentication or token validation on each call, no load balancer, gateway or service-mesh sidecar adding hops, no service discovery, and no real network latency, packet loss, retries or timeouts, and no cross-zone traffic. Real deployments have most of these. That makes the measured cost of splitting a floor for its network and security part, and the extra hops, handshakes and proxies come on top of every boundary you add.
  • Database servers on one machine. The headline figures use one shared PostgreSQL instance with a schema per module, so even the eight services shared one database server. That isolates the cost of the process boundary, which is the point of the comparison. Each split shape was also run with its own instance per deployable unit (three for groups, eight for the services) and it cost nothing measurable (groups 245 against 245 orders/s, microservices 161 against 159; the comparison). That is still on one machine, with every server sharing the same CPUs and loopback, and it does not charge the services for what real microservices usually add: a database server per service to provision, secure, back up, monitor and size, and a network path to each. So again the cost measured for the split shapes is a floor.
  • Cheap calls. The demo's calls are one primary-key query each, so the network share of an order is larger than in services that do real work per call. This pushes the other way, and is why the relative cost measured here may overstate what a heavy-calls domain would see. The two effects are real and run in opposite directions; measure your own journeys.
  • One domain and one workload. The demo's order flow and its order mix; a different domain or mix gives different call counts and different weights.
  • Run-to-run noise. The headline figures are means of 5 runs per mode; the cache, parallel and follow-up comparisons are single runs. Differences below about 5% are noise: the cache and parallel effects in the split modes are well above it, the outbox-versus-events difference is not.
  • No long-term operation. The measurements do not cover on-call load, incidents or a growing team. Those arguments come from the design and from the sprawl scenario, not from data.
  • Parked work. A few things the argument leans on are practices rather than shipped features: the cheap-module generator, the boundary-cost tool and a published-versus-internal API marker are in the parked ideas.
  • A default is not a ban. The claim is that microservices-first needs the analysis, not that it is never right.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Short definitions of the terms used across this site. Several of them sound alike, so the modes come first.

docs.title: Modes that are easy to confuse
docs.text:
Mode Artifact Processes Calls between modules PostgreSQL One-line meaning modulith app-modulith, a fixed all-in-one assembly 1 direct, in-process one instance, a schema per module every module in one process; the shape cannot be changed by configuration macro-modulith app-macro (the configurable jar), profile monolith 1 direct, in-process one instance the same all-local shape as modulith, built from the configurable jar. Every mode is built from modules, so there is no genuine monolith; each deployment has all modules enabled loopback-codec app-macro, profile loopback-codec 1 every call encoded to JSON-RPC and decoded, in memory one instance one process, but every call crosses a serialisation boundary loopback-http app-macro, profile loopback-http 1 every call a real HTTP request to the same process one instance one process, but every call crosses an HTTP boundary groups app-macro, profiles front, fulfilment, accounts 3 direct inside a group, JSON-RPC over HTTP between groups one instance a few processes, each hosting several modules split-dbs as groups 3 as groups three instances (A, B, C), one per group groups --dbs split: each group on its own PostgreSQL instance microservices eight app-<module>-service jars 8 all JSON-RPC over HTTP one instance, a schema per module; each service has its own schema, roles and pool one dedicated, generated jar per module microservices-macro app-macro run eight times, profile = module 8 all JSON-RPC over HTTP one instance, a schema per module; each process has its own schema, roles and pool the same eight processes, built from the single configurable jar

By default every mode except split-dbs uses one PostgreSQL instance with one schema per module, even the eight-process modes: separate processes do not mean separate database servers. Where a module's data lives is a separate choice (its datasource URL), and any module or group can be pointed at its own instance without a code change. --dbs split applies to any mode and gives every deployable unit its own instance (3 for the groups, 8 for the services, 1 for a one-process mode), so the layout follows the deployment; split-dbs is the name of groups --dbs split.

Only the two loopback modes put a serialisation or network boundary between modules that share a process. macro-modulith does not. Every mode serves the orders entry point and the shop on port 9181.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text: @Cached An annotation on an @RpcApi method that lets callers reuse its result for a short time. Applied to four read methods; switched off with rpc.cache.enabled=false or demo.sh --cache off. See the cache. @RpcApi The Java interface through which one module is called by another. A direct method call in the same process, a JSON-RPC 2.0 request when the module is elsewhere. It is the source of the server dispatch, the client proxies and the generated OpenAPI and OpenRPC documents. -api and -impl The two artifacts of a module: the @RpcApi interface with its data types and exceptions, and the implementation. A module may depend only on the -api artifacts of the modules it calls. Binding How a caller reaches a module: local (the implementation itself), loopback-codec, loopback-http or remote. It follows from what is enabled in the process. In call traces a call answered by the result cache is shown as binding cache, although that is not a configured binding. Boundary (logical and physical) A logical boundary is a module boundary the build enforces (contracts, schema, one-way dependencies). A physical boundary is a process, database instance or pipeline. A macro service has logical boundaries everywhere and physical ones only where they are needed. See principles. Boundary cost The calls per order that would cross a proposed boundary, multiplied by the extra cost of one remote call (about 1.0 to 1.7 ms on loopback here). A floor for the network part. See place modules by call weight. Call (module-to-module) One invocation of an @RpcApi method by another module. An order makes about 20. Closed loop The load pattern of the performance driver: each of N clients sends its next order as soon as the previous one returns. Crossing call A call between two modules that would be remote if a boundary were drawn between them. Declined order An order for a customer whose payment is always declined (2% of the seeded customers). An expected business outcome, reported separately, not a failure. Deployable Something built, started and released as a unit: a process type. A macro service is one image that can be deployed as one deployable or as several by configuration. Distributed monolith Services that must change and deploy together, so they have the costs of both models. What an early, wrong split tends to produce. Event publication registry Spring Modulith's store of events in the publisher's transaction (the orders.event_publication table), redelivered until their listener completes. Used when modules.orders.async=events. Follow-up A call to another module that must happen after an order changes state (release a reservation, void a payment, confirm to the customer). Made durable in the order's transaction and delivered after the commit, by the outbox or by events. See follow-up delivery. Group A set of modules hosted together in one process. The demo has front (orders, notifications), fulfilment (catalog, pricing, inventory, shipping) and accounts (customers, payments). Idempotent Safe to repeat. Calls that change state carry a request id derived from the order's, so a repeated or retried call causes one effect. Macro jar (app-macro) The one jar that contains every module and takes its shape from configuration: which modules a process enables and where the others are. Used by every mode except modulith and microservices. Macro service One team's bounded context, built from modules whose boundaries the build enforces, deployable as one unit or as several by configuration. It is not a monster monolith. Module The unit of code ownership: an -api/-impl pair with its own database schema and roles, its own connection pool and its own migrations, calling other modules only through their @RpcApi. Modulith (modular monolith) A single deployable divided into modules with enforced boundaries. Spring Modulith is the library used to verify the module structure; the modulith mode is the fixed all-in-one assembly of it. Monster monolith A shared, unenforced codebase for many teams, with shared tables and one release train, that keeps growing. The thing this project is not advocating. Outbox A table in the orders schema holding follow-ups written in the order's transaction, and a relay that delivers them with retries. The default, modules.orders.async=outbox. Parallel quotes The customer check and the two quotes at the start of placeOrder run at the same time. On by default; modules.orders.parallel-quotes=false or demo.sh --parallel off restores the sequential code. See parallel quotes. Percentiles (p50, p95, p99) The value below which 50%, 95% or 99% of the orders completed. p50 is the median order. Placement Which modules a process hosts, set by modules.<m>.enabled and the binding. The eight modes differ in placement. Profile (Spring profile) A named set of configuration. In app-macro, profiles such as monolith, front or orders choose the shape. Not the same as a workload profile. Replication and routing Replication is how many identical instances run; routing is which traffic reaches which instances. Both are independent of placement. See the levers. Published and internal API A planned distinction between an @RpcApi other teams may rely on and one only the owning team may use. Not implemented yet; see the parked ideas. Saga The orders.placeOrder flow: reserve, authorize, ship, capture, with compensations (release, void) when a step fails. The ordering is explicit in the orders module; there is no cross-module transaction. Schema and roles Each module has a PostgreSQL schema, a migration role that owns it and a runtime role with DML only on it. A module cannot read another module's tables. Slice A package-by-feature area inside a module. A practice, not a feature: the rules that keep slices independent are in the parked ideas. Version-skew pair A caller and callee that must stay compatible while they run different versions during a rollout. Zero inside one deployable, three between the demo's three groups, thirteen between eight services. Workload profile The customers, products and skew the load driver uses: small, realistic (default) or large. Not a Spring profile. See method.

docs.title: Principles: using a macro service well
docs.text:
How to decide what to build, where to draw boundaries, and what to deploy, for a team of 5 to 10 building a product. These are the working principles behind the design; the numbers come from the measurements and the module graph of the demo domain, and where something is a practice that the code does not yet support, it says so (parked ideas lists them).

The argument that follows from these principles is on the case page.

docs.title: 1. What a macro service is, and is not
docs.text:
A macro service is one team's bounded context, built from modules whose boundaries the build enforces, and deployable as one unit or as several by configuration. It is not a big monolith, and it does not mean "put everything in one deployable".

Macro service Monster monolith Microservices Scope one team's bounded context many teams, a whole company one narrow capability each Ownership one team of 5 to 10 nobody, or everybody one team per service Inside modules, build-enforced, no cycles packages, by convention process boundaries Data schema and roles per module, no shared tables shared tables and joins a database per service Contracts @RpcApi per module, compatibility-checked method calls and shared entities network APIs Release one unit per team one train for the company per service Growth bounded by guardrails, then another macro service unbounded sprawl inside a team Split-readiness proven continuously (loopback modes) unknown already split

What keeps it a macro service

  • A written scope statement: one bounded context, one owning team. A different bounded context is a different macro service, not one more module.
  • Boundaries that the build enforces: no cross-module table access, no cross-module transactions, an acyclic module graph, compatible APIs.
  • Budgets that trigger a review when crossed: team size, number of modules, build time, start-up time. These are guardrails to tune, not measured thresholds. For scale, the demo has 8 modules and its full build and tests take roughly 8 minutes.
  • Exit ramps agreed in advance: a second team, a diverging vocabulary, or a persistent release conflict means a second macro service, and the module graph shows where to cut. A company is then many macro services connected by published contracts.

docs.title: 2. Boundaries, placement, replication, routing and data are separate choices
docs.text:
Lever Question Set by Logical boundary what are the modules and their contracts? the code, enforced Placement which modules does a process host? modules.<m>.enabled and the binding Replication how many identical instances? the deployer Routing which traffic reaches which instances? an ingress, gateway or router Data placement which schema or database instance holds each module's data? the datasource URLs

The eight modes vary placement (with one replica). They are points in a larger space. A cluster of identical pods, each hosting every module, behind a router that sends /rpc/orders to one pool and /rpc/pricing to another, is also a deployment, and the database does not change.

Identical pods + routing Separate processes per module Hop on a module-to-module call none, it stays in-process a network hop, about 1.2 ms here Unit of version the pod the module Per-API scaling and canary yes, for externally entered calls yes, for all calls Version skew between modules none grows with the edges Moving parts one image, router rules N deployables

Things to know about routing:

  • It partitions entry traffic only. If orders runs in a pod, its calls to pricing run in that same pod whatever the router says about /rpc/pricing.
  • A canary is per pod, not per module, so a module-level canary seen by every caller needs that module as its own deployable.
  • Isolation is partial: a leaky module called internally still affects the pods it runs in.
  • With every module in every pod, every /rpc/<module> exists on every pod, so internal-only modules must be blocked at the ingress. The code has no published-versus-internal marker yet.
  • Connection pools are lazy and per module, so a pod only holds connections for modules it uses; the budget is about pods times active modules times pool size. Caches are per pod.
  • Running several replicas against one database has not been tested here. The outbox claims with a lease and the event registry resubmits with a compare-and-set, which looks designed for it.

docs.title: 3. Separate logically first, physically only when forced
docs.text:
Logical separation gives most of what a small team needs, at nearly no cost, and deployed as one unit it removes most of the operational burden.

Satisfied by logical separation (one deployable) Needs physical separation ownership, contracts, data ownership, dependency direction, independent tests, change locality, partitioned cognitive load independent release cadence, independent scaling, failure and resource isolation, a security or network zone, a different runtime, a vendor or other team owning the lifecycle

What one deployable costs you, measured on this domain: version-skew pairs 0 (against 3 for three groups and 13 for eight services), one image and pipeline, one database instance, and macro-modulith at the same throughput as modulith (442 against 445 orders/s).

What it does not give you: no CPU or memory isolation between modules (one leaky module affects all), one classpath, and one release unit, so a bad commit reaches everything. The controls are per-module bulkheads and connection pools, timeouts, asynchronous follow-ups, the runtime switches, and canarying the whole unit. If a requirement needs real isolation, that is a physical force, and you act on that module or group alone.

Split-readiness is a test, not a claim. loopback-codec in CI (98% of the throughput) passes only if no module relies on shared objects or a shared transaction, loopback-http adds a real HTTP hop, and a periodic microservices-macro run in staging proves the full split from the same artifact and shows its cost.

docs.title: 4. Start small and let boundaries appear
docs.text:
A new team should not begin with "how many services do we need?". Separate on evidence, merge on doubt.

Phase Work Output Understand the product outcomes, capability map, quality targets with numbers, what is unknown or volatile requirements with numbers, an uncertainty map Find the seams walk the top journeys; list the invariants (what must change atomically stays together), data ownership, integrations, what changes together candidate modules and the invariants not to split Score the forces the table below, with evidence "not yet" or "yes" for each candidate boundary Choose the start and the triggers pick the shape, write the extraction triggers, cost being wrong one-page decision record Instrument and revisit boundary metrics, a review cadence decisions driven by data Force Question Default for one team of 5 to 10 Release cadence must parts ship independently of each other? no: one team, one train Scale does a part need about 10 times the capacity? scale the whole thing; extract a measured hot spot Failure isolation must a failure in X not take down Y? bulkheads, timeouts and async follow-ups in-process Security or compliance is there an audit or network-zone boundary? separate schema and roles; extract only if the audit scope demands it Consistency which operations need atomic updates? keep them in one module and one transaction Ownership how many teams in 12 months? one team means one deployable Technology does a part need a different runtime? no Latency what is the end-to-end budget and call-chain depth? keep the hot path in-process Reuse does a second consumer exist? not until it does Operability can the team run N deployables and be on call for them? one

Cut by capability and by what must stay consistent, never by technical layer. A layered split (an API service, a business service, a data service) makes every feature a coordinated release. As an extrapolation from the measured per-hop cost (a lower bound on one machine), the demo's 20 calls per order each routed through two extra layer services would be about 60 hops, roughly +70 ms, against about +10 ms for the business-aligned groups split (8.4 crossing calls × 1.2 ms).

Boundaries can appear organically. Start with one module, or a few, and split as seams show up. For that to be cheap:

  • Inside a module, keep package-by-feature slices that are cycle-free, talk to each other through a small interface, and share no tables, so promoting a slice to a module later is mechanical.
  • Let the prototype show the seams: calls per journey across a candidate boundary, files that change together, and agreed triggers.
  • Creating a module has to be cheap. Today it is not: the documented procedure is nine manual steps touching the root pom, bootstrap.sql, 15 profile files in app-macro (72 "URL of the disabled module" lines in total) and more. That friction works against organic splitting and is the first item in parked ideas.

docs.title: 5. Changing a boundary later: splitting is easier than re-combining
docs.text:
The design work is the same in both directions and dominates the cost: decide who owns each table, remove joins, foreign keys and shared transactions across the line, and move or copy the data. In this codebase that is done by construction from day one: there are no cross-schema foreign keys (the only foreign key in any migration is inside inventory), the roles stop one module reading another's tables, and there are no cross-module transactions.

Move Mechanics Cost A table to another schema, same instance a metadata change (ALTER TABLE … SET SCHEMA), transactional, no copy very low A schema to another database instance copy the data (dump and restore, or logical replication), coordinate the cutover, flip the module's datasource URL moderate

The code change is one datasource property either way. The split-dbs mode proves only the code side, because its databases start empty.

Splitting Merging back Ownership creates it reconciles two owners Contract write an API at the cut remove it and inline its consumers Data already isolated per module collisions: every schema has its own flyway_schema_history, so merging schemas means merging migration histories and table names Consumers none or few yet everyone who adopted the API changes Organisation one team becomes two two teams must agree to become one

Merging is also less necessary: you can merge two modules' code and keep the schemas separate. The deployment level is symmetric and cheap (enable a module locally, or point it at a URL). The asymmetry is at the module level.

docs.title: 6. Place modules by call weight
docs.text:
Whether a call is a method call or a network hop depends only on whether the two modules share a process. In an a → b → c chain with one module per process, that is two sequential hops; with b and c together it is one.

All separateb and c together 
graph LR
  A1[a] ==>|"network"| B1[b] ==>|"network"| C1[c]
graph LR
  subgraph p["one process"]
    B2[b] --> C2[c]
  end
  A2[a] ==>|"network"| B2

The measurements show it. Keeping the chatty chains inside one process in groups cut the remote calls per order from 14.2 (eight services) to 8.4, and recovered 55% of the throughput (247 against 159 orders/s, 16 clients).

Cost of a boundary. Calls per order that would cross a boundary around each candidate, from the module call counts of one run (the 16-client microservices run, cache off). Each crossing call costs about 1.0 to 1.7 ms extra here (remote 1.5 to 2.2 ms against local about 0.5 ms; the table below uses 1.2 ms), on loopback, with no TLS, authentication or proxies, so a floor, against the about 20 calls of every order, which cost about 0.5 ms each in one process.

If you split out... Crossing calls/order About +ms per order Notes notifications 2.0 about 0 already asynchronous, off the request path payments 3.0 +3.6 also the strongest compliance reason pricing 4.0 +4.8 catalog 4.0 +4.8 cached reads, so less in practice customers 6.0 +7.2 five consumers; about half the calls are cache hits inventory 6.0 +7.2 chatty with shipping shipping with inventory 7.0 +8.4 the chain stays inside

The best grouping, computed. Every way of partitioning the 8 modules (4,140 of them) was scored by the calls per order crossing a boundary, and the minimum kept for each number of deployables:

Deployables Fewest remote calls/order, raw (cache off) After the cache 1 0 0 2 2.0 (notifications alone) 0.9 (catalog alone) 3 4.9 (notifications, payments, the rest) 2.5 (catalog, pricing, the rest) 4 8.0 4.3 8 19.9 14.2 demo groups (front, fulfilment, accounts) 10.9 8.7

Reading it:

  • The demo's grouping was chosen along team and domain lines, not by call weight, and is far from the minimum for three groups. A pure minimum peels off the weakly coupled leaves (notifications, payments, catalog), so those are the cheapest to extract.
  • The cache changes the answer. After caching, catalog is nearly free to separate, because most of its calls never leave the caller. Recompute the best grouping after tuning caches.
  • A minimum cut is one input. It ignores ownership, compliance, scaling and balance, so add those as constraints (for example, payments must be separate, shipping and inventory must stay together).
  • The weights depend on the order mix.
  • A prediction, not measured: a groups-style profile built on the computed cut should keep much more of the single-process throughput than the domain-based groups (56%).
How the numbers were computed

From the comparison.json saved by a perf.sh --modes ... --cache both run: for one run of microservices, the per-order call count of each caller→callee pair (count / orders; after the cache, (count - hits) / orders), then for every partition of the 8 modules the sum of the pair weights that cross a block.

weights[frozenset((caller, callee))] += (count - (hits if after_cache else 0)) / orders
# for each partition of the modules:  crossing = sum(w for pair, w in weights.items() if blocks differ)

docs.title: 7. Many teams: a macro service per team, contracts between them
docs.text:
For an organisation of many teams, the macro service is the team-level unit. Inside it, modules are the logical boundaries; between teams there are published, versioned contracts.

  • Version skew shrinks to the team boundary. Inside a team's macro service everything is one commit and one release unit. Only published APIs need independent compatibility.
  • Teams form a directed graph. Heavily used upstream teams (the demo's customers has five consumers) must publish stable, additive APIs with an SLA. Orchestrating teams (like orders, with six dependencies) are the fragile ones: use asynchronous follow-ups, timeouts and caches. Cycles between teams must be rejected, as the group graph must stay acyclic.
  • New features are modules by default. A new deployable needs a reason from the forces table.

Missing for this scenario: a published-versus-internal marker on @RpcApi, per-team artifact versioning and a registry of contracts with cycle and fan-in detection, cross-team asynchronous messaging (the design forbids a broker, and Modulith events are in-process), service-to-service authentication, discovery and canary routing, and wire-level contract tests between versions.

docs.title: Parked ideas
docs.text:
Not built, in roughly the order that would pay off:

  1. scripts/new-module.sh, which scaffolds a module (poms, schema and roles, datasource, profiles, ownership), plus a default-URL convention so a new module does not need a line in every profile.
  2. ArchUnit rules for slices inside a module (no cycles, one table per slice, no cross-slice joins).
  3. A "boundary radar": per-module coupling, cross-slice table use and files that change together.
  4. A boundary-cost script that scores a proposed grouping from traces (crossing calls and added latency) and searches for minimum-cost groupings under constraints, and a measurement of the prediction above.
  5. An exposure = INTERNAL | PUBLISHED attribute on @RpcApi, with an ArchUnit rule and japicmp on published APIs only.
  6. A --replicas N option and a small path router for demo.sh, to demonstrate and measure scale-out and routed pools, and to test several replicas against one database.
  7. A documented procedure for promoting a slice to a module, and for merging two modules.
  8. The organisation-level items in section 7.

docs.title: Project reference
docs.text: The detailed project notes that used to be the README: databases, raw JSON-RPC, the order-fulfilment domain, API documentation, hardening, layout and boundary rules. The newer material (modes, features, performance) has its own pages; this page is kept as a reference and some of it is older.

docs.title: Quick start: scripts/demo.sh
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh <mode> start      # reset PostgreSQL to a clean initialised state, build the jars on first use, start the mode, wait until ready
scripts/demo.sh <mode> status     # which processes are up
scripts/demo.sh <mode> stop       # stop the processes, then PostgreSQL

Modes: modulith, macro-modulith, groups, microservices, microservices-macro, loopback-codec, loopback-http, split-dbs. Only one mode runs at a time; start refuses while another is running. Logs and PID files are under .demo/.

The orders entry point and the shop are on 9181 in every mode:

  • Shop: http://localhost:9181/shop
  • Swagger UI: http://localhost:9181/swagger-ui
  • Topology: http://localhost:9181/demo/topology
  • JSON-RPC: POST http://localhost:9181/rpc/orders

Other processes: groups and split-dbs use 9181 front, 9182 fulfilment, 9183 accounts; microservices and microservices-macro use 9181-9188 (orders, catalog, pricing, inventory, customers, payments, shipping, notifications). Every start wipes and re-initialises the databases, so each run begins clean. Details: Running the demo modes.

docs.title: Performance: scripts/perf.sh
docs.text:
With a mode running (scripts/demo.sh <mode> start):

scripts/perf.sh                                  # 200 orders, 4 concurrent clients, 20 warmup orders
scripts/perf.sh --orders 1000 --concurrency 16
scripts/perf.sh --duration 60 --concurrency 8    # timed run instead of a fixed count
scripts/perf.sh --no-trace                       # client round trips only (least overhead)
scripts/perf.sh --modes groups,microservices     # start, measure and stop each mode on a clean database, then compare
scripts/perf.sh --modes all --orders 300         # all eight modes, one comparison table at the end

A realistic comparison (the realistic profile, which is the default), with the @Cached layer off and on, in two split modes:

scripts/perf.sh --modes groups,microservices --cache both --duration 120 --warmup 500 --concurrency 8

That starts each mode on a clean database, loads 10,000 customers and 2,000 SKUs, warms up with 500 orders, sends 120 s of load from 8 clients (about four times the cache TTL, so hit rates settle), stops the mode, and prints one comparison table. The run takes about 10 minutes (four measured runs plus start-up). The report is written to .demo/perf/<timestamp>/perf-<timestamp>.md. For a quick look at one running mode instead: scripts/perf.sh --orders 2000 --warmup 200 --concurrency 8.

The workload is the realistic profile by default: 10,000 customers and 2,000 SKUs with Zipf-skewed popularity (a few popular SKUs and repeat customers), 1-4 lines per order, 8% gold and 2% always-declined customers (declined orders are reported separately, not as failures). --profile small|realistic|large picks another (small = the demo's two customers and two SKUs, large = 100,000 and 20,000); --customers, --skus, --customer-skew, --sku-skew and --seed override. The driver bulk-loads the customers, products and stock first (--no-seed to skip), so every --modes run starts from a clean database. Use runs of at least three times the cache TTL (30 s) for meaningful hit rates.

It reports the client round trip of every orders.placeOrder (orders/s, error count, min/mean/p50/p90/p95/p99/max) and the latency of every module-to-module call inside those orders, grouped by caller -> callee.method and binding (local, loopback-codec, loopback-http, remote), plus calls per order. The call figures come from the /demo/trace records of every running process, so they are measured on the caller's side and include the JSON-RPC hop in the split modes. Raw samples (orders.csv, calls.csv) and summary.json go to .demo/perf/<timestamp>/ (one sub-directory per mode, plus comparison.json, with --modes).

Each run also writes a timestamped markdown report, perf-<timestamp>.md, next to the raw data: the parameters, commit, host, the comparison table across modes and, per mode, the round-trip and per-call tables. --cache on|off|both (with --modes) starts the modes with the @Cached layer on, off, or both, so you can compare them. --parallel on|off|both does the same for orders' parallel quotes (modules.orders.parallel-quotes).

Notes: the clients are a closed loop on persistent connections. Tracing adds a little overhead (compare with --no-trace). Each process keeps its 200,000 most recent calls (demo.trace.capacity), so a very long or fast run can still overwrite traces before they are read; the driver warns when that happens (raise the capacity or lower --concurrency). The demo seeds only 150 units of stock, so the driver raises it first (--no-stock to skip). Later async work (the notification, delivered by the outbox relay or an event listener) is picked up by re-reading traces until they stop changing (--settle, --drain).

docs.title: Caching: @Cached
docs.text: An @RpcApi method marked @Cached(ttlSeconds = 30, maxSize = 10_000) has its result reused by callers (a Caffeine cache per method, keyed by the arguments). It sits in front of every binding, local included, so a call costs the same wherever the module runs, and it is skipped for the one call the RPC dispatcher makes for a remote caller (that caller has its own cache). Failures and null results are never cached. Use it only for reads of slowly changing reference data: today customers.getCustomer, customers.getPaymentMethod, catalog.getProduct and catalog.productExists. Not for anything that changes state or reads fast-moving state (inventory.getStock, reservations). Results are shared between callers, so they must be immutable. Switch it off with rpc.cache.enabled=false (env RPC_CACHE_ENABLED=false). In the demo call trace a hit has binding cache.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: JDK 25, Maven 3.9+, Docker (from stage 4, for PostgreSQL and Testcontainers).

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
mvn -q verify                    # everything, including tests and boundary rules
mvn -q verify -pl modules/orders/orders-impl -am   # one module and what it needs
scripts/check-boundaries.sh      # proves the Maven boundary rules fail on forbidden dependencies

docs.title: Databases (stage 4)
docs.text:
Each module owns a schema, a DDL-capable migration role and a DML-only runtime role (docs/db/bootstrap.sql). Three PostgreSQL instances are available for the local demo (A 5432, B 5433, C 5434), each bootstrapped on first start:

docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml up -d --wait
docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml down -v        # stop and wipe

Persistence is JPA (Hibernate + Spring Data), one EntityManagerFactory and transaction manager per module, and Flyway per module (classpath:db/migration/<module>, plus classpath:db/demo/<module> seed data in the demo profile). A database that is down at startup does not stop the application: the module reports not-ready on /actuator/health/readiness and the migration is retried in the background. Liveness is unaffected.

Per-module pool settings (modules.<name>.datasource.*): max-pool-size (3), minimum-idle (0), idle-timeout (30s), max-lifetime (10m), connection-timeout (5s). platform.db.connection-budget warns when the enabled modules' pools add up to more (platform.db.enforce-budget=true fails startup). The RPC server limits concurrent calls per module to the pool size (modules.<name>.bulkhead.max-concurrent-calls, max-wait) and answers -32002 beyond that. Pool metrics: macro.db.pool.connections{module,state} and macro.db.pool.timeouts{module}.

docs.title: Shape 1: one process, one PostgreSQL
docs.text:
java -jar apps/app-modulith/target/app-modulith-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar --spring.profiles.active=demo --rpc.server.enabled=true
curl -s -X POST localhost:9181/rpc/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"orders.placeOrder","params":{"requestId":"m-1","customerId":"cust-standard","lines":[{"sku":"sku-widget","quantity":2}]},"id":1}'

(app-modulith serves no RPC by default; the override is only there so you can use curl.)

docs.title: Shape 2: eight services
docs.text:
orders.placeOrder needs seven other modules, so a split run starts all of them (scripts/demo.sh microservices start, or by hand, one app-<module>-service jar per module). Each service's application.yml already points at the default ports of the others.

scripts/demo.sh microservices start        # :9181 orders ... :9188 notifications
curl -s -X POST localhost:9181/rpc/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"orders.placeOrder","params":{"requestId":"s-1","customerId":"cust-standard","lines":[{"sku":"sku-widget","quantity":2}]},"id":1}'

docs.title: Raw JSON-RPC and the alias (stage 3)
docs.text:
# raw JSON-RPC 2.0 envelope (orders calls the other services over HTTP)
curl -s -X POST localhost:9181/rpc/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"orders.placeOrder","params":{"requestId":"req-1","customerId":"cust-standard","lines":[{"sku":"sku-widget","quantity":2}]},"id":1}'

# convenience alias: bare params in, bare result out (HTTP status carries errors)
curl -s -X POST localhost:9184/rpc/inventory/getStock -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"sku":"sku-widget"}'

app-modulith serves no RPC (rpc.server.enabled=false); app-macro runs all modules (monolith profile by default). Bindings per target module: modules.<name>.binding = local | loopback-codec | loopback-http | remote.

docs.title: The order-fulfilment domain (stage 5)
docs.text:
Eight modules, each with its own -api, -impl, schema, Flyway location and pool. They call each other only through @RpcApi interfaces (graph from section 16.1, checked exactly by DependencyGraphTests):

Module Calls catalog, customers none pricing catalog, customers inventory catalog payments, notifications customers shipping customers, inventory orders customers, pricing, shipping, inventory, payments, notifications

orders.placeOrder(requestId, customerId, lines) is a saga that lives in orders only: customer check, pricing quote, shipping quote, reserve stock, authorize payment, create shipment, capture, notify. The order state (PENDING -> RESERVED -> AUTHORIZED -> CONFIRMED, or REJECTED / FAILED) is persisted, every step is idempotent through a request id derived from the order's (<requestId>:reserve, :authorize, :ship, :capture), and a repeated call resumes where the order stopped. Compensations (inventory.release, payments.void) and the confirmation message are follow-ups, made durable in the same transaction as the state change and delivered after the commit. modules.orders.async picks the mechanism:

  • outbox (default): a row in the module's outbox table; a relay retries it with exponential backoff (modules.orders.outbox.*). The relay scans the database only when woken by a commit, while work is pending, or on a slow idle scan (idle-scan-interval, 60s), so an idle module holds no connection.
  • events: a Spring Modulith event (OrderEvents) stored by the event publication registry (orders.event_publication) and delivered by an asynchronous listener; a failed one is redelivered with exponential backoff (modules.orders.events.*). See docs/design/spring-modulith-events.md.

Either way a callee outage never fails the order. scripts/perf.sh --modes ... --async outbox|events|both compares them. The customer check and the two quotes run in parallel (modules.orders.parallel-quotes, default true).

payments.voidAuthorization is the design's payments.void (Java cannot name a method void).

Demo data (profile demo): products sku-widget (1000), sku-gadget (2500), sku-oos (no stock), sku-undeliverable (shipping always fails); customers cust-standard, cust-gold (10% off), cust-declined (card is declined). Amounts are cents.

call() { curl -s -X POST localhost:9181/rpc/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"method\":\"orders.placeOrder\",\"params\":{\"requestId\":\"$1\",\"customerId\":\"$2\",\"lines\":[{\"sku\":\"$3\",\"quantity\":$4}]},\"id\":1}"; echo; }
call happy-1      cust-standard sku-widget        2   # CONFIRMED, total 2700
call gold-1       cust-gold     sku-widget        2   # CONFIRMED, 200 off, total 2500
call oos-1        cust-standard sku-oos           1   # error 1001 OutOfStockException
call declined-1   cust-declined sku-widget        1   # REJECTED, reservation released by the relay
call undeliver-1  cust-standard sku-undeliverable 1   # FAILED, payment voided and stock released by the relay
call happy-1      cust-standard sku-widget        2   # same requestId: the same order, nothing duplicated

docs.title: Running the demo modes (stage 6)
docs.text:
Needs a JDK, Docker, curl and python3. The jars are built on first use (./mvnw -q -DskipTests package).

scripts/db.sh up                       # three PostgreSQL instances (A 5432, B 5433, C 5434), schemas and roles bootstrapped
scripts/demo.sh groups start             # any mode: modulith macro-modulith groups microservices microservices-macro loopback-codec loopback-http split-dbs
scripts/smoke.sh                       # the scenarios of section 16.5 + the expected binding on every edge + the merged call tree
scripts/trace.sh <correlationId>       # the merged call tree of one order, across every running process
scripts/demo.sh groups status
scripts/demo.sh groups stop
scripts/db.sh down                     # wipes the data
scripts/demo-all.sh                    # every mode on a clean database, with a summary table (pass/fail, bindings seen)
Mode Processes Cross-module path modulith app-modulith on 9181 all local macro-modulith app-macro (monolith) on 9181 all local groups app-macro as front 9181, fulfilment 9182, accounts 9183 local inside a group, remote across microservices the eight app-<module>-service apps on 9181-9188 all remote microservices-macro app-macro eight times, one module enabled each (profile = module name) all remote loopback-codec, loopback-http app-macro on 9181 every call through the JSON codec / over HTTP to 127.0.0.1 split-dbs as groups, profile split-dbs: front on A, fulfilment on B, accounts on C as groups

app-macro has no module wiring baked in; profiles do it (monolith, front, fulfilment, accounts, one per module, loopback-codec, loopback-http, split-dbs), or environment variables, for example MODULES_INVENTORY_ENABLED=false MODULES_INVENTORY_URL=http://host:9184/rpc/inventory. The eight service apps are generated from one template: scripts/new-service-app.sh --all (--check finds a stale one). app-modulith refuses to start with any module disabled or bound to anything but local.

With the demo profile (it implies dev) every process also serves:

Endpoint What GET /demo/topology per module: enabled, binding, URL, datasource host, port, schema (never the password) GET /demo/trace?correlationId=... the cross-module calls this process recorded: caller, callee, method, binding actually used, depth, duration, outcome POST /demo/faults {"notificationsDown":true,"paymentsDecline":true,"inventoryLatencyMs":300}; only applies to modules enabled in that process

Every placeOrder gets a correlation id (or takes X-Correlation-Id); it travels in the MDC, in the X-Correlation-Id header on remote calls and in the stored follow-ups, so the compensating calls stay attached to the order. Each call is also logged, for example pricing -> catalog.getProduct [local] 1 ms ok.

docs.title: API documentation (stage 7)
docs.text:
OpenAPI 3.1 and OpenRPC documents are generated at runtime from the @RpcApi interfaces (module platform/rpc-docs); nothing generated is committed. A process serves the documents of the modules it runs, only when rpc.server.enabled=true:

URL Content /rpc/{module}/openapi.json, /rpc/{module}/openrpc.json one module /rpc/openapi.json, /rpc/openrpc.json all modules of this process /swagger-ui Swagger UI, dev profile only (so also in demo) 
scripts/db.sh up && scripts/demo.sh macro-modulith start
open http://127.0.0.1:9181/swagger-ui        # pick "inventory", try inventory.getStock
curl -s localhost:9181/rpc/inventory/openapi.json | jq '.paths | keys'

Descriptions are optional: put @Operation(summary = ...) on a method, @Parameter(description = ...) on a parameter or @Schema(description = ...) on a record or component in the -api artifact (swagger-annotations-jakarta at provided scope; the annotations jar is on every runtime classpath through rpc-docs). Records are described as Jackson writes them: all components are required, and a component is nullable only if annotated with an annotation named Nullable.

mvn -pl apps/app-macro -am verify also writes the documents of all modules to apps/app-macro/target/api-docs/ (openapi.json, openrpc.json and one pair per module) for CI to publish.

docs.title: Hardening and compatibility (stage 8)
docs.text:
• Boundary interceptor. Calls to a local module behave like remote ones: they are observed as macro.rpc.client{module,method,binding,outcome} (the same series a remote call produces) and the caller's transaction is suspended for the call. Switch the suspension off with modules.boundary.suspend-transactions=false.
  • API compatibility. japicmp compares each -api jar with its last release and fails the build on removed or changed methods, constructors, record components and exception types; added methods pass. It is skipped until you name a baseline:
mvn verify -Dapi.compat.skip=false -Dapi.baseline.version=1.0.0     # the last released version, from your repository
scripts/check-api-compat.sh                                         # proves the check bites (compatible changes pass, breaking ones fail)

To add a field to a record without breaking Java callers, keep the old constructor and delegate to the new one. - Failure tests. ClientProxyFailureTests (timeout, refused or cut connection, JSON-RPC error, malformed answer, retry of an idempotent method) and DomainFailureTests (eight processes, callee killed mid-call, garbage answer, callee process restarted, orders process restarted with the outbox pending; always exactly one of every side effect).

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
