Path Purpose platform/rpc-api @RpcApi, RPC exceptions (no Spring) platform/module-support module stereotypes, enablement, per-module persistence helpers platform/rpc-spring-boot-starter JSON-RPC server, client proxies, registrar apps/demo-scenarios the section 16.5 scenarios and API contracts, written once against the -api artifacts (tests only) modules/<m>/<m>-api interface, record DTOs, exceptions; the only thing other modules may depend on modules/<m>/<m>-impl implementation, persistence, migrations platform/demo-support demo profile only: call trace, /demo/* endpoints, topology banner apps/* deployable assemblies (app-modulith, app-macro, app-<module>-service)

Platform code lives under io.macroservice.platform, outside the application root package com.acme, so that Spring Modulith does not treat it as a business module.

docs.title: Boundary rules (maven-enforcer-plugin)
docs.text:
• -api artifacts: only rpc-api and other -api artifacts at compile/runtime scope.
  • -impl artifacts: no other -impl, no app, no starter.
  • Service apps: only their own -impl.

docs.title: Adding a module
docs.text: Add modules/<m>/<m>-api and <m>-impl (copy inventory), list both in the root pom.xml <modules> and dependencyManagement, declare dependencies in the -impl pom and in @ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = ...), add the -impl to app-modulith and app-macro, and add a CODEOWNERS line.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: JDK 25, Docker (PostgreSQL runs in containers), curl and python3. Maven comes from ./mvnw.

docs.title: Start a mode
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh modulith start        # any mode: modulith macro-modulith groups split-dbs microservices microservices-macro loopback-codec loopback-http
scripts/demo.sh modulith status
scripts/demo.sh modulith stop         # stops the processes, then PostgreSQL

Four switches can be set when starting (they are ordinary properties, so environment variables and config files work too):

Option Values What it does --async outbox (default), events how orders delivers its follow-ups: the outbox relay or Spring Modulith events --cache on (default), off the @Cached result cache --parallel on (default), off the parallel customer check and quotes --dbs shared (default), split shared: one PostgreSQL instance with a schema per module. split: every deployable unit gets its own instance, so the layout follows the mode: groups 3 (A 5432 for front, B 5433 for fulfilment, C 5434 for accounts), microservices and microservices-macro 8 (one per module, ports 5432 to 5439). A one-process mode is one unit, so it stays on one instance. split-dbs is groups --dbs split 
scripts/demo.sh groups start --async events --cache off --parallel off
scripts/demo.sh groups status         # mode: groups   (async=events cache=off parallel=off wire=json dbs=shared)

start resets PostgreSQL to a clean, freshly initialised state every time (schemas and roles from docs/db/bootstrap.sql, migrations and demo data when the app boots), builds the jars on first use, starts the mode and waits until every process is ready. Only one mode runs at a time. Logs and PID files are under .demo/.

Look aroundPlace an orderTrace it URL What http://localhost:9181/shop the demo shop http://localhost:9181/swagger-ui generated API documentation http://localhost:9181/demo/topology modules, bindings and datasources of this process http://localhost:9181/actuator/health health 
curl -s -X POST localhost:9181/rpc/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"orders.placeOrder","id":1,
  "params":{"requestId":"r-1","customerId":"cust-standard",
            "lines":[{"sku":"sku-widget","quantity":1}]}}'

Demo data: customers cust-standard, cust-gold, cust-declined; SKUs sku-widget, sku-gadget, sku-oos (no stock), sku-undeliverable.

scripts/trace.sh <correlationId>       # the call tree of one order across every process
scripts/smoke.sh                       # seven scenarios, results and bindings asserted
scripts/demo-all.sh                    # every mode on a clean database, with a summary table

docs.title: Measure it
docs.text:
# a mode that is already running
scripts/perf.sh --orders 2000 --warmup 200 --concurrency 8

# start, measure and stop modes, with the result cache off and on, and compare
scripts/perf.sh --modes groups,microservices --cache both --duration 120 --warmup 500 --concurrency 8

# every switch: cache, parallel quotes, follow-up delivery
scripts/perf.sh --modes modulith,groups,microservices --cache both --parallel both --async both

# one shared PostgreSQL instance against one instance per deployable unit (both = shared and split)
scripts/perf.sh --modes groups,microservices --dbs both

Each run writes a timestamped markdown report with the modes side by side to .demo/perf/<timestamp>/. How the numbers are produced is in Method.

docs.title: Build and test
docs.text:
./mvnw clean verify          # everything, including boundary rules and the per-binding contract tests

The suite includes tests that start all eight services against real PostgreSQL containers, cut connections mid-call, and restart a process with work pending.

docs.title: Build this documentation
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve                                  # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mike deploy --push --update-aliases 0.1 latest      # publish a version to the gh-pages branch
mike set-default --push latest

mike keeps several versions on the gh-pages branch. That branch is its output: change the documents under docs/, never the built pages. Enable GitHub Pages for the repository with the source set to the gh-pages branch.

docs.title: Macro Service: A Spring Modulith Application Deployable as Monolith or Services
docs.text: Spring Boot 4 · Java 25 · Spring Modulith · PostgreSQL · JSON-RPC 2.0

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
A macro service is one Spring Boot codebase, built as one image, that runs as a single monolith or as several services depending only on configuration. Modules are Spring Modulith modules with strictly separated APIs. When two modules run in the same process they call each other directly. When they are split, the same Java interface is served and consumed over JSON-RPC 2.0. Each module owns its own PostgreSQL database and schema, on the same instance as other modules or on a different one.

JSON-RPC is the only inter-module interaction. The one way a module talks to another module is a call on that module's @RpcApi interface. When both modules are in the same process that call is a direct method call; when they are split it is a JSON-RPC 2.0 request. There is no other channel: no shared database access, no Modulith events, no message broker, no shared in-memory state, and no direct use of another module's internals.

The Java API interface is the single source of truth. Server dispatch, client proxies, OpenAPI and OpenRPC documents are all derived from it.

docs.title: 2. Goals, constraints and non-goals
docs.text:
Goals

  • One repository, one build, one image; the deployment shape is chosen by configuration.
  • Module boundaries are enforced at build time (Maven dependency rules, Spring Modulith verification), not by convention.
  • A module's @RpcApi interface is the only way another module may interact with it. The call is direct in-process and JSON-RPC 2.0 when the target module is not in the same process.
  • Each module configures its own PostgreSQL database and schema.
  • The Java API interface is the contract; OpenAPI and OpenRPC are generated and never edited by hand.

Constraints

  • Spring Boot 4, Java 25, Spring Modulith, PostgreSQL.
  • No cross-module database access, joins or transactions.
  • Module code never knows whether a collaborator is local or remote.
  • No channel between modules other than the @RpcApi call (see the table below).
Interaction between modules Allowed? Call another module's @RpcApi interface (direct in-process, or JSON-RPC when split) Yes, the only way Use another module's classes outside its -api artifact No (Maven and Modulith verification) Read or write another module's tables or schema No (separate roles and grants) Publish or listen to another module's Modulith or Spring events No (ArchUnit rule) Message broker, queue or topic between modules No Shared in-memory state, static singletons, shared caches No Shared transaction across modules No

Non-goals

  • Cross-module Modulith events, a message broker, or any asynchronous channel between modules.
  • Distributed transactions or two-phase commit.
  • Independent per-module versioning: every deployment runs from the same commit.

docs.title: 3. Architecture overview
docs.text:
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| One repo, one image: every module is built together          |
|   [ orders ]      [ inventory ]      [ platform ]            |
+------------------------------+-------------------------------+
                               | configuration selects the shape
              +----------------+-----------------+
              v                                  v
+---------------------------+      +-------------------------------+
| Monolith: one process     |      | Split: one process per service|
| [orders] -direct-> [inv.] |      | [orders] -JSON-RPC-> [inv.]   |
+---------------------------+      +-------------------------------+

The arrow between orders and inventory is the only interaction between the two modules in either shape. In the monolith profile, orders calls inventory as a direct in-process bean. In a split profile, the inventory bean is replaced by a JSON-RPC client proxy that talks to the inventory service. The module code does not change.

docs.title: 4. Repository and module layout
docs.text:
Each business module is split into an -api artifact and an -impl artifact in one multi-module Maven build. Only the -api artifact may be depended on by other modules.

repo/
  platform/
    rpc-api/                    @RpcApi, RpcException hierarchy (no Spring dependency)
    rpc-spring-boot-starter/    server dispatcher, client proxies, registrar, spec generator
    module-support/             per-module DataSource, Flyway, EMF helpers, @Module* stereotypes
  modules/
    orders/orders-api/          interface, record DTOs, exceptions
    orders/orders-impl/         implementation, persistence, module configuration
    inventory/inventory-api/
    inventory/inventory-impl/
  app/                          the macro service: Application class, profiles, all impls on the classpath
Artifact May depend on Contains <m>-api rpc-api, JDK; spring-modulith-api and swagger-annotations-jakarta at provided scope (annotations only, for @NamedInterface and @Operation/@Schema) @RpcApi interfaces, immutable records, unchecked exceptions <m>-impl own <m>-api, other modules' -api, module-support, Spring services, repositories, migrations, @ModuleConfiguration classes app all -impl artifacts, rpc-spring-boot-starter @SpringBootApplication at the root package, profile configs, health and readiness wiring

Because -impl artifacts depend only on other modules' -api artifacts, Maven rejects any attempt to reach another module's internals.

docs.title: 4.1 Packaging options
docs.text:
The module code is identical in every option. Only the assembly differs, so you can start with A and move to B or C later without touching the modules.

Option What you build What differs per deployment Choose it when A. One image, config-selected (the macro service) One app containing every -impl modules.<name>.enabled, datasource and client URLs You want the simplest pipeline, and image size and a union classpath do not matter B. Per-service assembly apps, same repo One app per service, each with only its own -impl plus other modules' -api Which jars are present, plus datasource and client URLs You want smaller images, or a guarantee that a service cannot run a module it should not C. Separate repositories and builds Each module builds and releases on its own and publishes its -api artifact for consumers Everything Teams need independent release cadences
  • A and B stay in one repository with lockstep versions: every artifact comes from the same commit, and an API change breaks every consumer's build immediately.
  • C gives up lockstep. Consumers depend on a published -api version, so the module owner must keep -api changes backward compatible across released versions (section 12, API compatibility check), as in any microservices setup.
  • In B and C, the startup validator and the registrar work unchanged: a module whose -impl jar is absent has no local bean, so its client proxy is registered and its URL is required.

docs.title: 5. Spring Modulith conventions
docs.text:
Modulith treats each direct sub-package of the application's root package as a module. It scans the classpath, so modules from separate Maven jars work as long as they share the root package (com.acme.orders, com.acme.inventory).

  • Named interface for the API. The api sub-package of each module is exposed with @NamedInterface("api"); everything else (internal) is hidden.
  • Declared dependencies. Each module lists what it may use, for example @ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = "inventory::api").
  • Verification in CI. ApplicationModules.of(Application.class).verify() fails the build on cycles, undeclared dependencies and access to non-exposed types.
  • @RpcApi is the only cross-module dependency. allowedDependencies may name only <module>::api, and an ArchUnit rule fails the build if any method annotated @ApplicationModuleListener, @EventListener or @TransactionalEventListener takes a parameter type that belongs to another module, or if an event type appears in a -api artifact. Cross-module use of anything other than an @RpcApi interface and its DTOs and exceptions is a build failure.
  • Documentation. Documenter generates the module canvas and component diagrams from the same model.
// inventory-api: com/acme/inventory/api/package-info.java
@NamedInterface("api")
package com.acme.inventory.api;

// orders-impl: com/acme/orders/package-info.java
@ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = "inventory::api")
package com.acme.orders;

Use the Modulith release line that matches Spring Boot 4 (2.x) and confirm it in the BOM before starting.

docs.title: 6. Module enablement
docs.text:
Because the image contains every module, Boot's component scan would register all of them. Enablement therefore has to be a property of the bean itself, not of an outer configuration class.

Module code uses module-aware stereotypes in place of @Service, @Component and @Configuration:

@Target(TYPE) @Retention(RUNTIME)
@Service
@Conditional(ModuleEnabledCondition.class)
public @interface ModuleService {
    String module();
}

class ModuleEnabledCondition implements Condition {
    public boolean matches(ConditionContext ctx, AnnotatedTypeMetadata md) {
        String module = (String) md.getAnnotationAttributes(ModuleService.class.getName()).get("module");
        return ctx.getEnvironment().getProperty("modules." + module + ".enabled", Boolean.class, false);
    }
}

@ModuleComponent and @ModuleConfiguration follow the same pattern. The persistence configuration (datasource, entity manager factory, repositories, Flyway) is a @ModuleConfiguration, so a disabled module has no connection pool, no migrations and no scheduled jobs, and the process never touches its schema.

Guard rails

  • An ArchUnit rule forbids plain @Service, @Component and @Configuration inside module packages.
  • Boot's single-datasource autoconfigurations (DataSourceAutoConfiguration, HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration, FlywayAutoConfiguration, JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration) are excluded, since each module defines its own.
  • A startup validator checks every @RpcApi interface: each module must be either enabled with a datasource, or disabled with a client URL. Otherwise the application fails to start, for example with Module 'inventory' is disabled but modules.inventory.url is not set.
  • Health indicators are registered only for enabled modules.

docs.title: 7. Inter-module communication: JSON-RPC is the only channel
docs.text: Every interaction between two modules is a call on the target module's @RpcApi interface. That call is a direct method call inside one process and a JSON-RPC 2.0 request between processes. Nothing else connects modules, and the build and the tests enforce it (sections 5 and 12).

docs.title: 7.1 One interface, two bindings
docs.text:
Consumers always inject the -api interface and cannot tell whether they received a local bean or a client proxy.

@RpcApi("inventory")
public interface InventoryApi {
    StockLevel getStock(String sku);
    Reservation reserve(ReserveRequest request);   // throws unchecked OutOfStockException
}

A BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor in rpc-spring-boot-starter runs after component scanning and handles every @RpcApi interface on the classpath:

  • A local implementation bean exists (the module is enabled): nothing is registered, and injection yields the direct in-process bean.
  • No local implementation (the module is disabled): a client proxy bean is registered that speaks JSON-RPC to modules.<name>.url. Startup fails if the URL is missing.
for (Class<?> api : findRpcApis()) {
    if (beanFactory.getBeanNamesForType(api, true, false).length == 0) {
        registry.registerBeanDefinition(beanName(api),
            BeanDefinitionBuilder.genericBeanDefinition(api, () -> proxies.create(api)).getBeanDefinition());
    }
}

The lookup uses allowEagerInit=false so it does not instantiate beans. Client proxies implement a marker interface so the server-side dispatcher never mistakes a proxy for a local implementation.

Rules for @RpcApi interfaces: no overloaded method names, immutable record parameters and results, unchecked exceptions only, and no types from outside the -api artifact.

docs.title: 7.2 No other channel: no events, no broker, no shared data
docs.text:
Modules communicate only through @RpcApi calls. A module may still use Spring or Modulith events internally, between its own components, but an event never crosses a module boundary. This removes the broker, the externalization and inbound-adapter configuration, and the event publication registry problem that arises when one registry has to serve several databases.

Where a module would previously have reacted to another module's event, it calls the other module's API instead, or the other module exposes a query that the first module polls.

docs.title: 7.3 Work that must survive a callee outage
docs.text:
Request/response means the caller depends on the callee being reachable. When a call must not be lost (for example, "tell inventory to release this reservation"), use a module-local outbox:

  • The caller writes an outbox row in its own schema in the same transaction as its business change.
  • A scheduled relay in the same module reads pending rows and calls the target @RpcApi method.
  • Target methods are idempotent, keyed by a request id carried in the call, so redelivery is safe.

This uses only the module's own database and the existing JSON-RPC path. Avoid Modulith's event publication registry for this: it is application-wide (one JdbcOperations), which does not fit a database per module.

docs.title: 7.4 Binding modes and loopback
docs.text:
Each module a consumer calls has a binding, set per target module with modules.<name>.binding. By default a local implementation bean wins; the other modes change what the registrar wires up.

Binding Path of a call Network Intended use local (default when the impl is present) Direct method call on the local bean None Production monolith loopback-codec Client proxy and dispatcher in the same JVM, through the JSON codec, no HTTP None Dev and test: catches DTOs that do not serialize cleanly (the rpc.loopback=true mode) loopback-http Client proxy over HTTP to 127.0.0.1, even though the impl is present Loopback interface Integration tests of the real HTTP path; not a production mode remote (default when the impl is absent) Client proxy over HTTP to modules.<name>.url Real network Split deployment 
modules:
  inventory:
    enabled: true
    binding: loopback-http
    url: http://127.0.0.1:9181/rpc/inventory

Rules:

  • loopback-codec and loopback-http register the client proxy even though the implementation is present, so the dispatcher must be able to find the local implementation. For loopback-http, rpc.server.enabled must be on.
  • loopback-http adds HTTP overhead and a self-call dependency on the server being up, so use it in tests, not in production.
  • Two separate services on one host or in one pod may simply use http://127.0.0.1:<port>/rpc/<module> as the remote URL. Nothing special is needed.
  • When /rpc is reached only over loopback, bind the endpoint to 127.0.0.1 (a separate rpc.server.address or port) so it is never exposed beyond the host. Service-to-service authentication is then not needed on that hop, but it is still required for any hop that crosses a network.
  • Startup validation rejects a loopback-* binding in any profile marked as production.

docs.title: 8. JSON-RPC protocol design
docs.text:
The protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP, implemented in the starter rather than taken from a library: the specification is small, and Boot 4 moves to Jackson 3 (tools.jackson), so check any candidate library for Jackson 3 support before adopting it.

Aspect Decision Endpoint POST /rpc/{module}, one per module, carrying the JSON-RPC envelope; batches and notifications supported Method name <module>.<method>, for example inventory.reserve; overloads rejected at startup Parameters By name (an object keyed by parameter name, compiled with -parameters), which evolves better than positional arrays Results The record returned by the Java method, serialized with Jackson 3 Errors Exceptions map to JSON-RPC error codes; the exception classes live in the -api artifact and are rehydrated on the client, so callers see the same exception types in both modes Client A java.lang.reflect.Proxy over RestClient with the JDK HttpClient; per-module timeouts and retry policy Context Trace identifiers and the caller's principal propagated in HTTP headers Security mTLS or signed service tokens between services; /rpc endpoints are not exposed publicly Threading Virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) so blocking remote calls stay cheap

The server side collects all local beans that implement an @RpcApi interface (excluding client proxies), builds a module.method index, and dispatches by reflection or method handles. The server can be switched off per deployment with rpc.server.enabled.

docs.title: 9. Persistence: database and schema per module
docs.text:
Each module owns its persistence configuration, bound to modules.<name>.datasource.*. A module with no explicit URL falls back to the shared spring.datasource, which gives "same instance, different schema" without extra settings.

  • Beans per module. A DataSource, EntityManagerFactory (or JdbcClient) and PlatformTransactionManager, each with an explicit bean name and none marked @Primary.
  • Repositories. @EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = "...orders.internal", entityManagerFactoryRef = "ordersEmf", transactionManagerRef = "ordersTm"), with @Transactional("ordersTm") on service code.
  • Migrations. A manually defined Flyway bean per module with its own locations (classpath:db/migration/orders), defaultSchema and history table inside the module's schema.
  • Schema and roles in PostgreSQL. One schema per module and one role per module with grants only on that schema; set the search path on the role (ALTER ROLE orders_app SET search_path = orders). Cross-schema joins then fail instead of creeping in.
  • Migration vs runtime roles. A migration role with DDL rights for Flyway, and a runtime role with DML only.
  • Connection pools (no external pooler). The design does not depend on PgBouncer or any other connection pooler, because AWS deployments cannot use one. Connections go straight from each application's pools to PostgreSQL, so the connection budget has to be managed by the application. See 9.1.

No module reads or writes another module's tables. Data owned by another module is obtained through its -api interface.

docs.title: 9.1 Connection budget without a pooler
docs.text:
This section matters for real AWS deployments. For the local demonstration (section 16) the pools can stay at their small defaults and the budget check can be left at warning level.

Each enabled module has its own Hikari pool, because each module uses its own role (and often its own instance). Different roles cannot share connections, so total connections grow with the number of enabled modules and with the number of application instances.

The budget

For each PostgreSQL instance:

sum over (enabled modules on that instance) of (maxPoolSize x application instances running that module) + migration and admin connections + reserve <= max_connections

  • max_connections on RDS and Aurora PostgreSQL is set by the parameter group and by default scales with the instance's memory, so read the real value (SHOW max_connections) rather than assuming one. Reserve some connections for superuser, monitoring and failover.
  • The same modules in a monolith and in services use the same total per module. The difference is where the pools live: a monolith holds all its module pools in one process, while a service holds only its own module's pool, multiplied by that service's instance count. Scaling a service out multiplies its pool, not the others'.

Application-level controls

  • Small pools by default. Set modules.<name>.datasource.max-pool-size per module, starting small and raising it from measured wait times, not from guesses.
  • No idle reservation. minimum-idle: 0 (or a low value), a short idle-timeout and a max-lifetime below any network or database idle limit, so an idle module holds no connections and a quiet service gives its connections back.
  • Lazy startup. Pools are created only for enabled modules (section 6), and do not fail startup on a slow database when the module is not in use.
  • Concurrency bulkhead. With virtual threads, thousands of requests can wait on a pool of a few connections. Put a per-module semaphore on the @RpcApi server side (and, if you wish, on the client) set equal to or slightly above the pool size, so excess requests queue in the application with a bounded wait and return a clear error rather than exhausting the pool or timing out deep in a transaction.
  • Short transactions. Never hold a connection across a call to another module; the boundary interceptor in section 11 already suspends the transaction on cross-module calls.
  • Budget check at startup. Each application reads platform.db.connection-budget (the connections this deployment may use on each instance, set per deployment) and logs a warning, or fails when platform.db.enforce-budget=true, if its enabled modules' max-pool-size values sum above it. The validator cannot know how many replicas run, so the deployment supplies the per-replica share.
  • Metrics. Expose each pool's active, idle, pending and timeout counts as Micrometer metrics tagged by module, and alert on pending threads and connection-acquire timeouts.

If the budget is still too tight

  • Use a larger database instance class (more max_connections), or move a busy module's schema to its own instance. Per-module datasource configuration already allows this with no code change.
  • Reduce the replica count and give each replica a larger pool, if the work is I/O bound on the database rather than the application.
  • If AWS RDS Proxy is allowed in your environment (it is a managed AWS service, not PgBouncer), it is an optional, configuration-only addition, because the application treats the database as an ordinary PostgreSQL endpoint. Check its behaviour with prepared statements and session settings such as search_path, which can pin connections, before relying on it. The design does not require it.
  • Sharing one pool across modules by switching roles on each checkout (SET ROLE) is possible but weakens the role-per-module isolation and adds per-checkout overhead, so it is not recommended unless the budget cannot be met any other way.

docs.title: 10. Deployment configuration
docs.text:
This section shows packaging option A (section 4.1): the same image is deployed N times with different configuration, selected by a Spring profile or by environment variables such as MODULES_INVENTORY_ENABLED=false. With option B or C the configuration is the same, except that a module whose -impl jar is absent needs no enabled: false, only its client URL. The binding modes in section 7.4 can be set per module in any profile.

# application-monolith.yml: every module in one process, separate schemas and instances
modules:
  orders:
    enabled: true
    datasource: { schema: orders }
  inventory:
    enabled: true
    datasource: { url: jdbc:postgresql://db2/inv, schema: inventory }

# application-orders-service.yml: orders locally, inventory over JSON-RPC
modules:
  orders:
    enabled: true
    datasource: { url: jdbc:postgresql://db1/app, schema: orders }
  inventory:
    enabled: false
    url: http://inventory:8080/rpc/inventory

# application-inventory-service.yml: inventory locally, orders is not needed
modules:
  orders:    { enabled: false }
  inventory:
    enabled: true
    datasource: { url: jdbc:postgresql://db2/inv, schema: inventory }
Deployment shape Enabled modules Calls between modules Monolith all direct in-process calls Orders service orders inventory.* over JSON-RPC Inventory service inventory none outbound (or JSON-RPC to others it consumes) Mixed grouping any subset in-process inside the group, JSON-RPC across groups

Startup validation rejects any deployment where a disabled module has no client URL or an enabled module has no datasource, so a misconfigured shape fails fast instead of failing on the first call.

docs.title: 11. Local vs remote parity risks
docs.text:
Because the @RpcApi call is the only inter-module interaction, it is also the only place where local and remote behaviour can differ. A call that is safe in-process can behave differently over the network, and these differences have to be designed out, because the same module code runs in both modes.

Risk Why it differs Mitigation Pass-by-reference vs serialization Local calls share object references; remote calls copy through JSON Immutable records for all DTOs; a rpc.loopback=true mode for dev and test that routes even local calls through the JSON codec Transactions A local call may join the caller's transaction on a shared datasource; a remote call never can No cross-module transactions; the boundary interceptor suspends the caller's transaction on local cross-module calls (modules.boundary.suspend-transactions, default true; see 17.2); module-local outbox (7.3) for cross-module consistency Failure modes Remote calls can time out, fail midway or be retried Idempotent mutating methods (client-supplied request id), timeouts and a retry policy on the client proxy Exceptions Remote errors pass through an error envelope Exception types defined in the -api artifact and rehydrated on the client Latency Chatty APIs are cheap in-process and costly over the network Coarse-grained API methods; no per-row calls in loops Observability Local calls leave no trace by default The same boundary interceptor observes local calls as macro.rpc.client, tagged exactly like remote calls (17.2) Security context The principal is implicit in-process Principal and trace headers propagated explicitly on remote calls

docs.title: 12. Testing strategy
docs.text:
The same test suites protect both deployment models, because the module code is identical in both.

  1. Structure. ApplicationModules.verify() plus the ArchUnit rules (stereotypes, no cross-module event listeners, no cross-module use of anything but @RpcApi types). These tests are what guarantee that JSON-RPC-capable calls are the only inter-module interaction.
  2. Module slices. @ApplicationModuleTest bootstraps a single module with its PostgreSQL schema (Testcontainers) and mocks its collaborators' -api interfaces, which is the same situation a split deployment creates.
  3. Contract tests. One test suite per -api artifact, run against each binding from section 7.4: local, loopback-codec (JSON round trip in-process), and loopback-http or remote against a started server. A failure in one binding but not the others is a parity bug.
  4. API compatibility. japicmp compares each -api artifact with its last released version and fails the build on removed or changed methods, constructors, fields (including record components) and exception types, to keep rolling deployments safe (see 14.3 and 17.2).
  5. Deployment smoke tests. Start the image with each profile (monolith, each service) and call one method per module through the public API, including one call that crosses a module boundary.
  6. Startup validation tests. Assert that each broken configuration (missing URL, missing datasource) fails with the expected message.

docs.title: 13. API documentation: OpenAPI and OpenRPC
docs.text:
The Java interface is the source of truth, so generated documents cannot drift from the code. JSON-RPC does not map cleanly onto OpenAPI because every call is a POST to one URL, so the design uses two complementary outputs.

  • OpenAPI. Generated at runtime from the @RpcApi interfaces. Implementation note (stage 7): swagger-core (2.2.55, the latest) and springdoc (3.1.1, which targets Boot 4) both still depend on Jackson 2 (com.fasterxml.jackson); no release supports Jackson 3. The record schemas are therefore generated by the rpc-docs module itself, following Jackson's record conventions, and the Swagger annotations are read by name. Swagger UI comes from the org.webjars:swagger-ui webjar, without springdoc. One operation per method at POST /rpc/{module}/{method}.
  • Path alias on the server. The same POST /rpc/{module}/{method} path is also served: bare params object in, bare result out, no envelope. This makes Swagger UI and curl usable, while the real protocol remains the JSON-RPC envelope on /rpc/{module}.
  • OpenRPC. The native description format for JSON-RPC, emitted from the same reflection model; the more faithful document for client generators.
  • Endpoints. /rpc/{module}/openapi.json per module, and a merged document for deployments that run several modules.
  • Descriptions. Optional @Schema and @Operation annotations on the API interfaces.

No spec file is committed or edited by hand. If a spec is needed as a build artifact, a build step generates it from the compiled -api artifact.

docs.title: 14. Development process compared with standard microservices
docs.text: "Standard microservices" here means each service is an independently built, versioned and released component, usually with its own repository, pipeline and client library for its neighbours.

docs.title: 14.1 Side by side
docs.text: Concern Macro service Standard microservices Repository and build One repository, one multi-module build, one image A repository (or independent build) per service, N images Local development Run the monolith profile in one JVM with one debugger session; only PostgreSQL is external Run several services plus dependencies, or rely on stubs, Docker Compose or a shared dev cluster Cross-module refactoring IDE rename and move across modules; one commit; the compiler checks every consumer Coordinated changes across repositories, published client libraries, deprecation periods Changing an API A breaking change fails the build of every consumer immediately; compatibility is still required between deployed versions Consumer-driven contracts or versioned endpoints; compatibility maintained across independently released services Dependency and library upgrades One BOM and one upgrade; all modules move together; one classpath that is the union of all modules Per-service, independent; versions drift between services CI pipeline One pipeline; affected modules built with -pl <module> -amd; smoke test per profile N pipelines plus a contract broker and integration environments Test confidence Module slice, contract and profile smoke tests in one run; full system test is starting the monolith profile End-to-end tests across deployed services; slower and more prone to flakiness Release One commit produces one image; each deployment is that image with different configuration Each service releases on its own cadence with its own version Database migrations Flyway per module, reviewed in the same repository; each module still migrates only its own schema Per-service repository and migration pipeline Debugging and tracing In the monolith, ordinary stack traces; once split, distributed tracing Distributed tracing needed from day one Ownership CODEOWNERS per module directory; Modulith verification guards boundaries Repository ownership; strong team autonomy Technology freedom One language, runtime and Spring version Per-service choices, including other languages Blast radius of a bad change A bad commit can reach every deployment built from it; mitigated by per-service rollout and profile smoke tests A bad release affects only that service Patching and security One image to scan and patch N images Scaling and failure isolation Available once split, through configuration Native

docs.title: 14.2 Day-to-day workflow
docs.text:
1. Develop against the monolith profile: one process, direct calls, one database instance with a schema per module.
  2. Change a module's API: the build immediately shows every consumer that breaks, and they are fixed in the same commit.
  3. Run verify(), the ArchUnit rules, module slice tests and the contract tests for the changed -api artifacts.
  4. CI builds one image and starts it once per profile (monolith and each service shape), running the smoke tests.
  5. Deploy: each service runs the same image with its profile. A service whose module and dependencies did not change can skip the redeploy.
  6. Split further by configuration only: enable another module in a service, or move it to its own service by adding a URL and a profile.

docs.title: 14.3 Differences that still matter
docs.text:
• Version skew during rollout. In a rolling deployment, a service on the new commit calls a service still on the old one. Changes to -api artifacts must be additive for the length of the rollout (add fields and methods, deprecate, then remove in a later release), and the compatibility check in section 12 enforces it. This discipline is the same one microservices need, only the window is shorter, because everything ships from one commit.
  • The shared classpath. Every module's dependencies are on every deployment's classpath, so one module's library choice affects all of them. Per-service assembly modules (section 4) remove this when it becomes a problem.
  • Distributed monolith risk. If cross-module calls are chatty or modules share tables, splitting will be painful in either model. The schema-per-role setup (section 9) and coarse-grained APIs (section 11) are the controls.

docs.title: 14.4 When standard microservices are the better fit
docs.text:
• Many teams need genuinely independent release cadences, rather than one lockstep commit.
  • A component needs a different language, runtime or major framework version.
  • Regulatory or organizational boundaries require separate repositories, access control or pipelines.
  • Dependency sets differ so much that a union classpath is unworkable.

The macro service is the better fit when one team or a small group owns all the modules, refactoring across module boundaries is frequent, and the option to split later matters more than independent releases today. Splitting later is a configuration and deployment change; moving to full microservices later means giving each -api/-impl pair its own repository and pipeline, which the layout in section 4 already supports.

docs.title: 15. Trade-offs, risks, open questions and next steps
docs.text:
One artifact, config-selected (this design) Per-service assembly modules Build outputs 1 jar / image N jars / images Classpath Union of all modules' dependencies Only the modules a service needs Boundary enforcement Build time plus runtime configuration Build time (absent jars) Operations One image deployed N ways N pipelines Main risk A misconfigured deployment runs a module it should not (startup validation mitigates) Slightly more build and release plumbing

Risks to retire early

  • JSON-RPC and OpenAPI generation must be confirmed to work with Jackson 3 in Boot 4.
  • ~~Decide whether the boundary interceptor that suspends transactions on local cross-module calls is enforced or left to convention.~~ Decided in stage 8: enforced by default, switchable (17.2).
  • Callers now depend on callee availability for every cross-module interaction; decide which calls need the module-local outbox (7.3).
  • No connection pooler is available on AWS, so the per-module pool sizes, replica counts and the database's max_connections must fit the connection budget (9.1). Work this out per environment before the first multi-module deployment.

Open questions

  • What service-to-service authentication is standard here: mTLS, signed tokens or a service mesh?
  • Should per-module databases always use separate roles, or only in production?
  • Is lockstep release (one commit, one image) acceptable for every module, or does any module need a different cadence?

Next steps

  • [ ] Scaffold the repository: platform, two sample modules (orders, inventory) and the app.
  • [ ] Implement the @Module* stereotypes, the condition and the startup validator.
  • [ ] Implement the JSON-RPC server dispatcher, client proxy and registrar, with loopback mode.
  • [ ] Implement the per-module PostgreSQL, Flyway and transaction-manager configuration.
  • [ ] Add the ArchUnit rules (stereotypes, no cross-module event listeners) and the -api compatibility check.
  • [ ] Add contract tests and profile smoke tests for the monolith and split shapes.

docs.title: 16. Local demonstration
docs.text: The immediate goal is to demonstrate every deployment mode on one developer machine, from the same code, using a domain with real interdependence between modules. Everything runs on localhost, PostgreSQL runs in Docker, and the demo profile (which implies dev) enables the helpers below. Service-to-service security, cloud configuration and image publishing are out of scope for the demo.

docs.title: 16.1 Demo domain: order fulfilment
docs.text:
Eight modules. Each has its own -api and -impl, its own schema, and calls other modules only through their @RpcApi interfaces.

Module Responsibility Main API methods Calls (through their APIs) catalog Products and base prices getProduct(sku), productExists(sku) none customers Customer profile, tier, address, payment method reference getCustomer(id), getPaymentMethod(id) none pricing Quotes with tier discounts quote(customerId, lines) catalog, customers inventory Stock and reservations getStock(sku), reserve(orderId, lines), release(reservationId), getReservation(id) catalog payments Authorize, capture, void authorize(requestId, customerId, amount), capture(authId), void(authId) customers shipping Shipping quotes and shipments quote(customerId, lines), createShipment(orderId, customerId, reservationId) customers, inventory notifications Customer messages (logged to its own schema; no real email) send(requestId, customerId, template, params) customers orders The orchestrator and the public entry point placeOrder(requestId, customerId, lines), getOrder(orderId) customers, pricing, shipping, inventory, payments, notifications 
graph LR
  orders --> customers
  orders --> pricing
  orders --> shipping
  orders --> inventory
  orders --> payments
  orders --> notifications
  pricing --> catalog
  pricing --> customers
  inventory --> catalog
  shipping --> inventory
  shipping --> customers
  payments --> customers
  notifications --> customers

The graph has fan-out (orders calls six modules), chains three calls deep (orders -> shipping -> inventory -> catalog), and diamonds (orders reaches customers directly and through pricing, payments and shipping). It must stay acyclic: Modulith verification rejects module cycles, and a cycle between two @RpcApi interfaces would also make startup and call ordering fragile. If two modules appear to need each other, extract the shared concern into a third module that both call.

orders.placeOrder flow (a saga with compensation)

  1. customers.getCustomer validates the customer.
  2. pricing.quote prices the lines (it calls catalog.getProduct for each line and customers.getCustomer for the tier discount).
  3. shipping.quote prices delivery (it calls customers.getCustomer for the address and inventory.getStock for the warehouse, which calls catalog.productExists).
  4. inventory.reserve reserves stock. Failure: the order is rejected with an out-of-stock error and nothing else has happened.
  5. payments.authorize for the total plus shipping. Failure (declined): inventory.release, order REJECTED.
  6. shipping.createShipment. Failure: payments.void and inventory.release, order FAILED.
  7. payments.capture, order CONFIRMED.
  8. notifications.send through the orders module's outbox, so a notifications outage never blocks or fails the order (section 7.3).

Compensating calls (release, void) are written to the orders outbox in the same transaction as the order state change and retried by the relay, with idempotent targets keyed by request id. All ordering of calls is explicit in orders; there is no cross-module event and no cross-module transaction.

docs.title: 16.2 Groupings
docs.text:
Because modules can be grouped into processes in any combination, the demo defines these named groupings. A grouping is just a set of enabled modules plus URLs for the rest.

Group Modules Port in groups mode front orders, notifications 9181 fulfilment catalog, pricing, inventory, shipping 9182 accounts customers, payments 9183 Edge Inside one group (direct call) Across groups (JSON-RPC) orders -> notifications yes (front) pricing -> catalog, inventory -> catalog, shipping -> inventory yes (fulfilment) payments -> customers yes (accounts) orders -> pricing, shipping, inventory front -> fulfilment orders -> customers, payments; notifications -> customers front -> accounts pricing -> customers; shipping -> customers fulfilment -> accounts

The grouping graph is front -> fulfilment -> accounts and front -> accounts, which is acyclic. A module graph with no cycles can still produce a cycle between groups (for example, if customers were in fulfilment and shipping in accounts). That is legal at runtime, but each group then needs the other's URL and readiness gets harder, so choose groupings that keep the group graph acyclic.

docs.title: 16.3 Ports and databases
docs.text: Item Port Notes All-in-one app 9181 modulith, macro-modulith and the loopback modes Group processes 9181 front, 9182 fulfilment, 9183 accounts groups and split-dbs modes One process per module 9181 orders, 9182 catalog, 9183 pricing, 9184 inventory, 9185 customers, 9186 payments, 9187 shipping, 9188 notifications microservices and microservices-macro modes PostgreSQL A 5432 shared instance, one schema per module PostgreSQL B, C 5433, 5434 extra instances for split-dbs (front on A, fulfilment on B, accounts on C)

docs.title: 16.4 Demo modes
docs.text:
Mode Artifact(s) run Processes Cross-module path Databases modulith app-modulith 1 all local A, eight schemas macro-modulith app-macro, profile monolith 1 all local A groups app-macro three times, profiles front, fulfilment, accounts 3 mixed: local inside a group, remote across groups (table in 16.2) A microservices eight per-service apps (app-<module>-service) 8 all remote A microservices-macro app-macro eight times, one module enabled each 8 all remote A loopback-codec app-macro, profile loopback-codec 1 every call through the JSON codec in-process A loopback-http app-macro, profile loopback-http 1 every call over HTTP to 127.0.0.1:9181 A split-dbs as groups 3 as groups front on A, fulfilment on B, accounts on C

Per-service apps contain their own -impl plus the -api artifacts of the modules they call, which is exactly that module's allowedDependencies. An enforcer rule checks that an app's declared -api dependencies match it, so a service app cannot silently depend on more than its module may use.

docs.title: 16.5 Scenarios the demonstration runs in every mode
docs.text:
The same smoke script runs against every mode, calls orders.placeOrder on whichever process hosts orders, and must produce identical results and exception types:

Scenario Trigger Expected outcome Happy path, standard customer cust-standard, in-stock SKUs CONFIRMED; price with no discount Tier discount through the chain cust-gold CONFIRMED; lower total (shows orders -> pricing -> customers) Out of stock SKU sku-oos rejected with OutOfStockException; no payment calls in the trace Payment declined with compensation cust-declined REJECTED; trace shows inventory.reserve then inventory.release Shipping failure with two compensations SKU sku-undeliverable FAILED; trace shows payments.void and inventory.release Dependency down notifications toggled down with POST /demo/faults order still CONFIRMED; notification delivered by the outbox relay after the fault is cleared Idempotent retry same requestId sent twice one order, one reservation, one authorization

Seed data (products, customers, stock) comes from demo-only Flyway migrations in each module's own location, loaded only in the demo profile.

docs.title: 16.6 Demo aids
docs.text:
• GET /demo/topology lists, for the modules in that process, whether each is enabled, its binding (local, loopback-codec, loopback-http, remote), the target URL if any, and the datasource host, port and schema (never the password).
  • Call trace with correlation: every placeOrder gets a correlation id that is propagated in an HTTP header and in-process. GET /demo/trace?correlationId=... returns that process's recorded cross-module calls (caller, callee, method, binding actually used, duration, outcome, depth). The same data is logged one line per call, for example pricing -> catalog.getProduct [local] 1 ms ok.
  • scripts/trace.sh <correlationId> queries every running demo process and prints one merged call tree, with the binding shown on each edge, so the chain orders -> shipping -> inventory -> catalog is visible as a single tree whether it ran in one process or four.
  • POST /demo/faults (demo profile only) turns a module's failures on or off: notifications down, payments decline, inventory latency. It affects only modules enabled in that process.
  • Startup banner prints the topology when the process starts.
  • Scripts: scripts/db.sh up|down (PostgreSQL containers, roles and schemas), scripts/demo.sh <mode> start|stop|status, scripts/smoke.sh, scripts/trace.sh, and scripts/demo-all.sh (every mode in turn with a pass/fail summary table).

docs.title: 16.7 What the demonstration should show
docs.text:
1. The module code and the API interfaces are identical in every mode; only the artifact and configuration change.
  2. The only interaction between modules is the @RpcApi call, and the merged trace shows each edge's binding change between local, loopback-* and remote as the grouping changes.
  3. A chain of dependent calls (orders -> shipping -> inventory -> catalog) behaves identically whether it runs in one process or across several.
  4. Each module keeps its own schema, and in split-dbs each group its own database instance, with no code change.
  5. A module's database role cannot read another module's schema, even when all eight are in one process.
  6. Failures in the middle of the chain compensate correctly (release, void) and a dependency being down does not fail the order.
  7. Results and exception types are identical across all modes.

docs.title: 17. Implementation notes and deviations
docs.text: Where the implementation differs from the sections above. Each item was either removed or is recorded here.

docs.title: 17.1 Decisions that differ from the text above
docs.text: Area Design said Implementation Why Persistence API Not fixed Spring Data JPA/Hibernate per module, each module with its own DataSource, Flyway, EntityManagerFactory and transaction manager (<module>Tm), none @Primary User decision Versions Two-week-old releases Spring Boot 4.1.2 and Spring Modulith 2.1.2, released days before use User waived the rule for these two Platform package root com.acme Platform code is under io.macroservice.platform.*, outside the application root, so Modulith does not treat it as a module Keeps ApplicationModules limited to business modules payments.void void voidAuthorization void is a Java keyword; the table is payment_authorization and money is in cents -api dependencies rpc-api and JDK Also spring-modulith-api and swagger-annotations-jakarta at provided scope (annotations only) @NamedInterface and optional @Operation/@Schema descriptions OpenAPI schemas swagger-core model converters Generated by platform/rpc-docs No swagger-core or springdoc release supports Jackson 3 (13) Demo prerequisites Docker and a JDK Also curl and python3 for the scripts; Maven comes from ./mvnw The scripts post JSON and merge traces app-modulith in the demo No RPC server The demo profile enables it on 127.0.0.1 only; ModulithGuard still rejects a disabled module or a non-local binding The smoke test needs an HTTP entry to orders; calls between modules stay direct Disabled modules in app-macro Not stated Every disabled module on the classpath needs a URL, even one this process never calls The registrar builds a proxy per @RpcApi Call trace (demo) One interceptor demo-support wraps every @RpcApi bean, records the edge on the caller side only, finds the caller module from the call stack, and carries the depth in X-Rpc-Depth Exact edges and the same tree in every mode Boundary interceptor An AOP interceptor A BeanPostProcessor that wraps each local @RpcApi implementation in a JDK proxy at lowest precedence (outside the callee's own @Transactional proxy) Needs no pointcut and works for the dispatcher too

docs.title: 17.2 Stage 8: boundary parity, compatibility and failure behaviour
docs.text:
• Boundary interceptor. Every local @RpcApi implementation is wrapped. A call through it (a) is observed as macro.rpc.client with tags module, method, binding, outcome (and error on failure), the same name and tags a remote call gets from its client proxy, so a timer exists per binding and a tracing bridge makes it a span; and (b) suspends an active transaction (PROPAGATION_NOT_SUPPORTED semantics, on every PlatformTransactionManager) unless modules.boundary.suspend-transactions=false. When the dispatcher invokes the bean for a looped-back or remote caller, only (b) applies; the caller's proxy has already recorded the call. Consequences: a local implementation is no longer injectable by its concrete class (only by its @RpcApi interface, which the module rules already require), and boundary is a reserved name under modules.* (the modules map binds it as an empty module, which is harmless).
  • Metrics instead of a tracer extension. Metrics and tracing live in the production-path interceptor, not in the demo-only call tracer, so they exist in every profile; the demo tracer is unchanged.
  • Compatibility check. japicmp-maven-plugin runs at verify in every -api module and is skipped until a baseline exists. CI runs mvn verify -Dapi.compat.skip=false -Dapi.baseline.version=<last release>; the baseline is resolved from the configured repositories like any dependency. Binary-incompatible changes break the build; a method added to an interface does not (additive on the wire). Adding a record component changes the canonical constructor and is reported; keep the old constructor (delegating with a default) to make it pass. Known gap: renaming a method parameter keeps Java compatibility but changes the JSON field name; the generated OpenRPC document changes in that case and should be diffed in review. scripts/check-api-compat.sh proves the check bites.
  • Failure behaviour. The client proxy maps a timeout, a refused or cut connection, HTTP 502/503/504 and -32001/-32002 to RpcUnavailableException; a malformed, empty, mismatched-id or mistyped answer and the codes parse error, invalid request, method not found and invalid params to RpcProtocolException; a declared @RpcError to the same exception type; any other error to RpcRemoteException. Only @Idempotent methods are retried, only after an unavailable failure, at most modules.<m>.client.retries times. DomainFailureTests runs the eight modules as eight processes with a fault-injecting proxy in front of payments, shipping and notifications.
  • Outbox relay. A relay now makes its first scan five seconds after it starts (modules.orders.outbox.startup-scan-delay), so entries left pending by a process that died are delivered promptly instead of after a full idle-scan interval (found by the relay-restart test). The delay keeps a freshly started, idle module free of database connections for that moment.

docs.title: Discussion: Spring Modulith async calls and events
docs.text: Status: historical. This was written for discussion on the branch discuss/spring-modulith-async; parallel quotes and the switchable follow-up delivery it led to are now on main (see parallel quotes and follow-up delivery). Its measurements are from 4-client runs on the former small JVMs and are not the numbers on the performance pages.

docs.title: Where we are
docs.text:
• Modules talk only through @RpcApi interfaces: a direct call in-process, JSON-RPC when split. Request/reply, one transport model.
  • The order saga (OrdersService) is explicit and synchronous: reserve, authorize, ship, capture. There is no cross-module event and no cross-module transaction, by design.
  • The only asynchronous work is hand-built: compensations and the confirmation notification are written to an outbox table in the order's transaction, and OutboxRelay delivers them later by calling the target module's @RpcApi (idempotent by request id, retried with backoff). Because it goes through @RpcApi, it works unchanged in every binding.
  • Spring Modulith 2.1.2 is already in the BOM (spring-modulith-api in module-support), used today for module structure and docs, not for events.

docs.title: What Spring Modulith offers
docs.text:
• @ApplicationModuleListener: an @Async, transactional (REQUIRES_NEW) event listener; the module-to-module event idiom.
  • Event publication registry (JDBC): publications are stored in the publisher's transaction and marked complete when the listener finishes; incomplete ones are re-submitted (on restart, or on demand). This is the outbox pattern as a library.
  • Event externalization (@Externalized): the same event is also sent to Kafka, AMQP, JMS and so on, which is how events cross processes.
  • Integration-test support for modules (Scenario), and verification that listeners respect module boundaries.

docs.title: What "async" could mean here (they are different things)
docs.text:
1. Replace our outbox with the event publication registry. Same guarantee, less code. OutboxRelay is a candidate.
  2. Events instead of calls for side effects. OrderConfirmed published by orders; notifications (and later others) listen. Orders would no longer depend on NotificationsApi.
  3. Parallel or non-blocking request/reply (futures, virtual threads) inside the saga. This is not a Modulith feature, but it is where the latency is: see below.
  4. Full choreography (each step reacts to the previous step's event). Removes the orchestrator.

docs.title: What the measurements say
docs.text:
From scripts/perf.sh (realistic profile, microservices, cache off): p50 round trip about 65 ms. The serial calls the saga makes average: shipping.quote 5.6 ms, createShipment 4.2, pricing.quote 4.0, payments.authorize 2.7, inventory.reserve 2.1, payments.capture 1.4, customers.getCustomer 0.9. The notification (about 3 ms) is already off the request path.

  • Option 2 (and 1) therefore do not shorten the critical path; they change structure and reliability, not latency.
  • Option 3 could: pricing.quote, shipping.quote and getCustomer are independent and could run in parallel.
  • @Cached already removes some read latency (+20-30% orders/s in the split modes).

docs.title: Spike result: parallel quotes (option D)
docs.text:
Implemented on this branch: placeOrder runs customers.getCustomer, pricing.quote and shipping.quote at the same time on virtual threads (io.macroservice.platform.rpc.Parallel), joining in the old order so callers see the same exception as before. Thread-bound context (logging MDC, the demo trace depth) is carried into the workers. modules.orders.parallel-quotes=false restores the sequential code. Measured with scripts/perf.sh --modes modulith,groups,microservices --parallel both --orders 2000 --warmup 300 --concurrency 4 (realistic profile, @Cached on, one machine, so a loopback hop is about 2 ms):

Mode orders/s off to on p50 ms p95 ms p99 ms modulith 351 to 357 (+2%) 11.0 to 10.9 16.2 to 15.9 18.4 to 18.0 groups 210 to 234 (+11%) 18.0 to 16.6 (-8%) 28.1 to 24.7 (-12%) 31.3 to 27.7 (-12%) microservices 154 to 182 (+18%) 24.7 to 21.0 (-15%) 38.7 to 33.4 (-14%) 45.2 to 37.3 (-17%)
  • It helps where the calls are remote and does nothing in-process, as predicted. About 15% off the median in microservices.
  • Throughput also rose, because at 4 clients the machine is not CPU-bound and the saga was waiting on hops. At saturation (many clients) the gain will shrink. Worth repeating at 16 or 32 clients.
  • No change to what a caller can observe: same results, same exceptions, same number of calls (the unit tests and the full build pass).
  • Cost: one small helper and a context-propagation rule that every thread-bound facility (MDC, trace depth) must follow. Anything new that is thread-bound and matters to a call (security context, transaction) has to register with Parallel or must not be used inside a parallel call.

docs.title: Tensions with the current design
docs.text:
• Process boundaries. Modulith events are in-JVM. In groups / microservices an event crosses processes only via externalization (a broker) or by delivering it as an @RpcApi call, which is what the outbox does today. A broker is a new moving part for a demo that today needs only PostgreSQL.
  • One database schema per module with separate migrator and runtime roles. The JDBC registry wants an event_publication table; here it would have to live in each publishing module's schema, with grants for both roles, and use that module's DataSource and transaction manager (we have one EntityManagerFactory and transaction manager per module, not a shared one).
  • Explicit ordering and compensation. The saga's state machine is readable and testable; choreography spreads it across listeners.
  • The "no cross-module event" rule is currently a stated property (and checked by the architecture tests). Events would need a rule of their own.
  • Tracing and perf tooling. /demo/trace, CallTracer and perf.sh record @RpcApi calls; an event hand-off would need the same.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Effect Cost / risk A. Keep as is Nothing changes None; hand-built outbox stays B. Registry replaces OutboxRelay Less code, standard behaviour Per-module schema and transaction manager wiring; retry/backoff semantics differ C. Events for notifications (+ externalization if split) Orders no longer depends on notifications Needs a broker or RPC-delivered events in split modes D. Parallel reads in the saga (futures / virtual threads) Real latency win on the critical path Context propagation (MDC, trace depth, transactions); not Modulith E. Choreography No orchestrator Hardest to reason about and to compensate; loses request/reply semantics

docs.title: Questions for the discussion
docs.text:
1. Is the goal reliability and less code (B), decoupling (C), or latency (D)? They need different work.
  2. Do we accept a broker for split modes, or must the demo stay PostgreSQL-only?
  3. Should events be a second, explicit channel next to @RpcApi, and what stops it growing into hidden coupling?
  4. Is the explicit saga a feature we want to keep? (I would keep it.)
  5. Does each module keep owning its own event table and roles?

docs.title: Suggested spike
docs.text: On this branch: switch only the notification hand-off to an @ApplicationModuleListener with the JDBC registry in modulith and macro-modulith modes, behind a property, keep OutboxRelay for the split modes, and compare with scripts/perf.sh --modes (including the failure behaviour when notifications is down). Separately, prototype D on pricing.quote + shipping.quote and measure.

docs.title: Spring Modulith events instead of the hand-built outbox
docs.text: Status: historical; both branches are now merged into main (see follow-up delivery), and the measurements below are 4-client runs on the former small JVMs, not the numbers on the performance pages. Branches spike/spring-modulith-events (replaces the outbox) and spike/switchable-async (keeps both, modules.orders.async=outbox|events, default outbox). The events model is Spring Modulith 2.1.2's own: domain events, the event publication registry, and asynchronous transactional listeners. Everything else (the synchronous saga, @RpcApi calls, per-module schemas and roles) is unchanged.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• OrderEvents: three events (ReleaseReservation, VoidPayment, OrderConfirmed) published by OrderStore inside the transaction that changes the order, and a Listeners component that calls the other module through its @RpcApi. Because it goes through @RpcApi it works in every binding, including split processes.
  • Modulith's registry stores each publication in orders.event_publication in that same transaction, marks it PUBLISHED / PROCESSING / COMPLETED / FAILED / RESUBMITTED, and PersistentApplicationEventMulticaster runs the listener after commit.
  • OrdersEventListener: @Async + @TransactionalEventListener, i.e. Modulith's @ApplicationModuleListener without its @Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW) (see "friction").
  • OrderEventRedelivery: decides when a failed publication is resubmitted (exponential backoff, max attempts).
  • OrdersEventPublicationRepository: the event store over the orders pool (see "friction").
  • Flyway V2__event_publication.sql drops outbox and creates Modulith's schema v2 table in the orders schema.
  • Removed: OutboxRelay, OutboxRepository, OutboxEntryEntity, OutboxSignal, OutboxCommand, the outbox table.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Realistic profile, 2,000 orders, 4 clients, cache on, same flags on main (outbox) and on this branch:

Mode Orders/s outbox / events p50 ms outbox / events p99 ms outbox / events modulith 351 / 333 11.1 / 11.7 18.1 / 20.6 groups 210 / 213 18.4 / 18.3 31.2 / 30.6 microservices 156 / 154 24.7 / 24.7 42.7 / 47.5

The request path is the same, so the round trip is within noise (modulith about 3-5% slower on this run; one run each, not repeated).

Delivery of the asynchronous work is very different. 1,000 orders placed flat out, then the time until every notification reached notifications.message: events 0.1 s after the last order, outbox (main) 48 s. The old relay claims 20 entries per one-second poll (about 20 per second); that is a tuning limit of our relay, not of the outbox pattern, but the registry plus an async executor needs no such tuning.

docs.title: Friction (what it cost to fit Modulith's model to this project)
docs.text:
1. One transaction manager per module. The registry's own methods are @Transactional with no qualifier, so with eight transaction managers the context fails. ordersTm is now @Primary. That is correct only because orders is the one module that publishes events; a second publishing module would need a second registry (Modulith assumes one).
  2. Modulith's JDBC repository does not fit. It is package-private, wants a single primary DataSource and opens a connection at start-up to detect the database. Our pools never connect at start-up (an unreachable database must not stop the process; a test enforces it). So OrdersEventPublicationRepository reimplements the repository (same table, same statements, completion mode UPDATE only) over the orders pool.
  3. @ApplicationModuleListener cannot name a transaction manager, and our listeners only call other modules, so holding an orders connection open while they call would waste the pool. We use the same annotation without the @Transactional.
  4. Every process that contains orders-impl gets Modulith's event auto-configuration, which refuses to start without a repository. EventPublicationStandIn (module-support) provides a stand-in that fails loudly when orders is not hosted. (A first attempt that excluded the auto-configuration from an EnvironmentPostProcessor broke on test property timing, and one placed in the orders package was filtered out by @ApplicationModuleTest.)
  5. The retry policy is ours. The registry stores, marks failures and can resubmit, but it has no backoff, no maximum attempts and no schedule. OrderEventRedelivery supplies them. To keep "an idle module holds no database connection" it scans only after a failure, shortly after start (crash recovery) and on a slow idle scan; Modulith's staleness monitor and republish-on-restart were not used because they query the database on a timer or at start-up.
  6. Multi-instance: markResubmitted is a compare-and-set claim, so two instances do not resubmit the same publication, but redelivery to a listener whose first attempt is still running is possible; targets are idempotent by request id, as before.
  7. Noise: every failed delivery logs an ERROR with a stack trace from Spring's async exception handler.
  8. Events do not cross processes by themselves. Here that does not matter because the listeners call @RpcApi; moving the notification into the notifications module as a listener (so orders no longer depends on it) would need externalization to a broker.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text: Equal on the critical path, far better at draining asynchronous work, and the saga stays explicit. Costs: a custom repository, a custom redelivery policy, a primary transaction manager and a stand-in bean, i.e. Modulith's registry is usable here but only after adapting it to the one-schema-per-module design. If a second module needs events, the primary-transaction-manager approach stops working.

docs.title: Making it switchable (spike/switchable-async)
docs.text: OrderStore publishes follow-ups through a small port, FollowUps. OutboxFollowUps (default) turns them into outbox rows; EventFollowUps publishes Modulith events. The components of the unused mechanism are not created (@ConditionalOnProperty on the relay, the listeners, the redelivery policy and the event repository), both tables exist (outbox from V1, event_publication from V2), and an unknown value fails at start-up (AsyncModeCheck). The saga and failure tests run once per mechanism (OutboxOrderSagaTests / EventsOrderSagaTests, OutboxDomainFailureTests / EventsDomainFailureTests). Costs of keeping both: Modulith's event auto-configuration, the primary ordersTm and the stand-in repository bean are present even in outbox mode, and a few hundred lines of code for the mechanism that is not selected.

docs.title: Staged Claude Code prompt: macro service
docs.text:
How to use this file:

  1. Put the design document in the repository as docs/design/macro-service.md.
  2. Start Claude Code in the repository root and paste the Master prompt once.
  3. Paste one stage prompt at a time. Do not move on until the stage's definition of done is met and you have reviewed the commit.
  4. If Claude Code wants to deviate from the design, it must stop and ask, as the master prompt requires.

docs.title: Master prompt (paste first, once)
docs.text:
You are building the "macro service" described in docs/design/macro-service.md. Read that file completely before doing anything else. It is the authoritative design. Where this prompt and the design disagree, stop and ask me.

What we are building, in short:
- One Spring Boot 4 / Java 25 codebase using Spring Modulith and PostgreSQL, built with Maven (multi-module reactor).
- Business modules are split into <module>-api and <module>-impl artifacts. Only -api artifacts may be depended on by other modules.
- JSON-RPC 2.0 is the ONLY interaction between modules. When two modules are in one process, the call is a direct method call on the @RpcApi interface; when they are split, it is a JSON-RPC request. No cross-module events, no broker, no shared tables, no shared state, no shared transactions.
- Each module owns its own PostgreSQL database/schema, configured under modules.<name>.datasource.*, with its own Flyway migrations.
- The Java @RpcApi interface is the source of truth. OpenAPI and OpenRPC are generated from it.
- From the same code we build several app artifacts: app-modulith (all impls, all local, RPC server off), app-macro (all impls, fully config-driven), and per-service apps such as app-orders-service and app-inventory-service (only their own impl plus other modules' -api).

Build plan: stages 1 to 4 prove the mechanism with two pilot modules (orders, inventory). Stage 5 grows them into the full eight-module demo domain with real interdependence (section 16.1 of the design). Stage 6 builds the local demo harness around that domain.

Working agreement:
1. Work in stages. I will give you one stage at a time. Do only that stage.
2. Before writing code in a stage, state your plan in a few lines, including any decision you are making that the design leaves open.
3. Do not guess dependency versions. Look up the current Spring Boot 4 release and the matching Spring Modulith, Flyway, Testcontainers, ArchUnit and springdoc/swagger-core versions from authoritative sources (Maven Central, release notes) and use the BOMs. Record the chosen versions in the parent POM. Pick versions at least two weeks old.
4. Boot 4 uses Jackson 3 (package tools.jackson). Do not pull in Jackson 2 or a JSON-RPC library that requires it. Implement JSON-RPC ourselves in the starter.
5. Never use an implementation class of another module. Never add a dependency from one -impl to another -impl. If you think you need to, stop and ask.
6. Keep each stage small and reviewable. At the end of each stage: run `mvn -q verify` from the root, fix everything, then make one git commit with a message starting "stage N:". Do not start the next stage.
7. At the end of each stage, report: what you built, decisions you made, anything you could not do, and the exact commands I can run to verify it.
8. Use the placeholder root package com.acme (modules are com.acme.orders, com.acme.inventory). I will rename it later.
9. Prefer records for DTOs, constructor injection, and no Lombok.
10. We deploy on AWS and cannot use PgBouncer or any external connection pooler. Never design for or depend on one. Connections go straight from each module's HikariCP pool to PostgreSQL, and the application manages its own connection budget (see section 9.1 of the design).
11. The immediate target is a LOCAL DEMONSTRATION of the deployment modes on one developer machine (see section 16 of the design). Optimise for a clear, repeatable demo: everything runs on localhost, PostgreSQL runs in Docker, the dev profile allows loopback bindings, and security between services is out of scope for now. Do not build production-only machinery (cloud deployment, image publishing, service-to-service security) unless a stage asks for it.

Reply with a short summary of your understanding of the design (maximum 15 lines) and the list of open questions you have. Do not write code yet.

docs.title: Stage 1: Repository skeleton and build
docs.text:
Stage 1: repository skeleton and build.

Create the Maven reactor and empty modules. No business logic yet. Orders and inventory are the two pilot modules used to prove the mechanism in stages 1 to 4; the other six modules of the demo domain are added in stage 5, so structure everything so that adding a module is mechanical.

Layout:
  pom.xml                         parent POM + BOM imports (Spring Boot 4, Spring Modulith), Java 25, -parameters, enforcer rules
  platform/rpc-api
  platform/rpc-spring-boot-starter
  platform/module-support
  modules/orders/orders-api
  modules/orders/orders-impl
  modules/inventory/inventory-api
  modules/inventory/inventory-impl
  apps/app-modulith
  apps/app-macro
  apps/app-orders-service        (orders-impl + inventory-api)
  apps/app-inventory-service     (inventory-impl)
  docs/design/macro-service.md   (already present)

Requirements:
- Dependency rules enforced by Maven: -api artifacts depend only on rpc-api and the JDK; -impl artifacts depend on their own -api, other modules' -api, module-support and Spring; apps depend on impls/apis and the starter. Use the maven-enforcer-plugin (banned dependencies / dependency convergence) so that an orders-impl -> inventory-impl dependency fails the build. Add a short check that proves it fails.
- Each app has a @SpringBootApplication class in the single root package com.acme and an application.yml. The apps must start (even if they do nothing yet).
- Add package-info.java files with @NamedInterface("api") on com.acme.orders.api and com.acme.inventory.api, and @ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = "inventory::api") on the orders module where appropriate.
- Add .gitignore, a root README with build instructions, and a CODEOWNERS file with one line per module directory.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes from the root.
- Temporarily adding an orders-impl -> inventory-impl dependency makes the build fail (show me, then revert).
- Each app jar starts and exits cleanly when run with --spring.main.web-application-type=none.
- Versions chosen are listed in your report with where you got them.

docs.title: Stage 2: RPC API, exceptions and module stereotypes
docs.text:
Stage 2: rpc-api and module-support. Still no network code.

In platform/rpc-api (no Spring dependency):
- @RpcApi("name") annotation (type-level, runtime retention) naming the module.
- RpcException hierarchy: a base unchecked exception with an error code, plus RpcUnavailableException (remote unreachable or timed out), RpcProtocolException (malformed request/response), and RpcRemoteException (unexpected server error).
- An @RpcError(code = ...) annotation for business exceptions defined in -api artifacts, so they can be rehydrated on the client.

In platform/module-support:
- @ModuleService, @ModuleComponent and @ModuleConfiguration stereotypes, each with a module() attribute, each meta-annotated with the matching Spring stereotype and @Conditional(ModuleEnabledCondition.class).
- ModuleEnabledCondition reading modules.<name>.enabled (default false).
- ModuleProperties (@ConfigurationProperties "modules") exposing enabled, url, binding and datasource settings per module.
- A startup validator (ApplicationRunner or SmartInitializingSingleton) that, for every @RpcApi interface found on the classpath, checks: if the module is enabled it has a datasource (own or shared spring.datasource); if it is disabled or has no local implementation bean it has a client URL. It fails startup with a clear message such as "Module 'inventory' is disabled but modules.inventory.url is not set".

In the sample modules:
