- inventory-api: InventoryApi (@RpcApi("inventory")) with getStock(String sku) and reserve(ReserveRequest request); records StockLevel, ReserveRequest, Reservation; OutOfStockException annotated with @RpcError.
- orders-api: OrdersApi (@RpcApi("orders")) with placeOrder(PlaceOrderRequest request) and getOrder(String orderId); records and one business exception.
- Stub implementations in the -impl modules using @ModuleService, returning in-memory values for now.

Add ArchUnit tests in platform (shared test-jar) that every app inherits:
- Classes in module packages may not use plain @Service, @Component, @Configuration (must use the @Module* stereotypes).
- Event listener methods (@ApplicationModuleListener, @EventListener, @TransactionalEventListener) may not take parameter types from another module.
- Cross-module access may only reference types in a module's api package.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes.
- Unit tests prove: a disabled module's beans are absent; the validator fails with the expected message for each broken configuration; each ArchUnit rule fails when a violating class is added in a test fixture (show the negative tests).
- app-modulith starts with all modules enabled and the stub implementations wired.

docs.title: Stage 3: JSON-RPC server, client proxy, registrar and bindings
docs.text:
Stage 3: the JSON-RPC layer in platform/rpc-spring-boot-starter. Implement it ourselves with Jackson 3.

Server:
- POST /rpc/{module} accepting a JSON-RPC 2.0 envelope. Support single requests, batches and notifications (no id). Return correct JSON-RPC errors for parse error, invalid request, method not found, invalid params and internal error.
- Method name is "<module>.<method>". Build the method index at startup from all local beans implementing an @RpcApi interface, excluding client proxies (use a marker interface on proxies). Reject overloaded method names at startup with a clear message.
- Parameters by name (an object keyed by parameter name; requires -parameters). Results are the returned record.
- Exceptions: a business exception annotated @RpcError becomes a JSON-RPC error with its code and a data object carrying the exception class name and message; anything else becomes an internal error without leaking stack traces.
- Also serve POST /rpc/{module}/{method} as a convenience alias: bare params object in, bare result out, no envelope.
- Switchable with rpc.server.enabled. Bind address configurable with rpc.server.address.

Client:
- A java.lang.reflect.Proxy over RestClient (JDK HttpClient) that builds the envelope, sends it to modules.<name>.url, and maps errors back: @RpcError codes rehydrate the exact exception type from the -api artifact; transport failures become RpcUnavailableException. Per-module connect/read timeouts and an optional retry policy (off by default, safe only for idempotent methods).
- Propagate trace headers and the caller's principal as headers; leave security wiring as an extension point.

Registrar and bindings:
- A BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor that scans the classpath for @RpcApi interfaces and, per module, applies the binding from modules.<name>.binding: local (default when an impl bean exists), loopback-codec (proxy that routes through the JSON codec and the dispatcher in-process, no HTTP), loopback-http (proxy over HTTP to 127.0.0.1 even though the impl is present), remote (proxy over HTTP to modules.<name>.url; the default when no impl bean exists).
- Use beanFactory.getBeanNamesForType(type, true, false) so beans are not instantiated during the check.
- Startup validation rejects loopback-* bindings when a profile named "prod" or "production" is active, and fails fast on missing URLs.

Tests:
- Dispatcher tests for every JSON-RPC error case, batches and notifications.
- A contract test base class parameterised by binding that exercises InventoryApi.getStock and reserve (including OutOfStockException) against local, loopback-codec, loopback-http and remote (two Spring contexts in one test, one serving and one calling over a random port). Results and exceptions must be identical across bindings.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes, including the contract tests for all four bindings.
- I can start app-inventory-service and app-orders-service locally and see orders call inventory over JSON-RPC (give me the curl for one raw JSON-RPC request and the alias path).

docs.title: Stage 4: Per-module persistence, PostgreSQL and Flyway
docs.text:
Stage 4: per-module persistence with PostgreSQL, using Testcontainers.

In platform/module-support:
- A helper to build, from modules.<name>.datasource.* (url, username, password, schema, pool size), a HikariCP DataSource, and fall back to the shared spring.datasource when a module sets no URL (same instance, different schema).
- A helper to build the module's Flyway bean: locations classpath:db/migration/<module>, defaultSchema = the module's schema, history table inside that schema, creating the schema if needed. Support a separate migration credential (modules.<name>.datasource.migration-username/password) falling back to the runtime credential.

In orders-impl and inventory-impl:
- A @ModuleConfiguration that defines that module's DataSource, Flyway, JPA EntityManagerFactory (or JdbcClient if simpler; state which you chose and why) and transaction manager, with explicit bean names (ordersDataSource, ordersTm, ...) and none marked @Primary. Repositories are scoped to the module's own package with explicit EMF and transaction manager refs; services use @Transactional("ordersTm").
- Exclude Boot's single-datasource autoconfigurations (DataSource, HibernateJpa, Flyway, JpaRepositories) in the apps.
- Replace the in-memory stubs with real persistence: inventory has stock and reservations tables; orders has an orders table. A migration per module under its own folder.

Connection budget (no external pooler; see section 9.1 of the design):
- Pool settings per module under modules.<name>.datasource: max-pool-size, minimum-idle (default 0), idle-timeout, max-lifetime, connection-timeout. Defaults must be small.
- Pools are created only for enabled modules, and must not fail application startup when the module's database is temporarily unreachable (configure Hikari accordingly and make readiness reflect it, not liveness).
- A budget check at startup: read platform.db.connection-budget (connections this deployment may use per instance) and log a warning if the sum of enabled modules' max-pool-size exceeds it; fail startup instead when platform.db.enforce-budget=true.
- A per-module concurrency bulkhead (semaphore) in the RPC server dispatcher sized from the module's max-pool-size, with a bounded wait and a clear JSON-RPC error when exhausted (stage 3's dispatcher gets a hook for this; add it here).
- Micrometer metrics for each pool (active, idle, pending, timeouts) tagged by module.

Rules:
- No module reads another module's tables. orders gets stock via InventoryApi only.
- Provide an SQL bootstrap script (docs/db/bootstrap.sql) creating, per module, a schema, a migration role and a runtime role with grants only on that schema and search_path set on the role.

Tests:
- Testcontainers PostgreSQL: one instance with two schemas, and one test with two separate instances, proving both layouts work with only configuration changes.
- A test that the runtime role of orders cannot select from the inventory schema.
- Budget tests: a disabled module opens no connections (check pg_stat_activity); with minimum-idle 0 an idle module holds none; the budget check warns, and fails with enforce-budget=true, when pool sizes exceed the budget; the bulkhead returns the documented error under load while the pool is exhausted, without deadlocking.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes (Docker available).
- app-modulith runs against a single PostgreSQL with both schemas; app-orders-service and app-inventory-service run against different instances; the same placeOrder flow works in both shapes (give me the commands, including docker compose for the databases).

docs.title: Stage 5: Demo domain with interdependent modules
docs.text:
Stage 5: grow the two pilot modules into the eight-module order-fulfilment domain in section 16.1 of the design. The platform (stages 1 to 4) must not change except where a gap is found; if it must change, tell me why first.

Modules (each with <m>-api and <m>-impl, own schema, own Flyway location, own persistence configuration from stage 4):
  catalog, customers, pricing, inventory, payments, shipping, notifications, orders
Dependencies (and nothing else) are exactly the "Calls" column of the table in section 16.1. Declare them in each module's package-info (@ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = ...)) and in each -impl pom. The graph must be acyclic; add a test that fails if a cycle or an undeclared dependency appears.

APIs (records for all DTOs; unchecked exceptions annotated @RpcError in the -api artifact; every mutating method takes a requestId and is idempotent):
- catalog: getProduct(sku), productExists(sku).
- customers: getCustomer(customerId) (tier, shipping address, email), getPaymentMethod(customerId).
- pricing: quote(customerId, lines): base price from catalog, tier discount from customers.
- inventory: getStock(sku) (validates the SKU via catalog), reserve(requestId, orderId, lines), release(requestId, reservationId), getReservation(reservationId).
- payments: authorize(requestId, customerId, amount), capture(requestId, authId), void(requestId, authId); looks up the payment method through customers.
- shipping: quote(customerId, lines) (address from customers, warehouse from inventory), createShipment(requestId, orderId, customerId, reservationId).
- notifications: send(requestId, customerId, template, params): resolves the email address through customers and records the message in its own schema; no real email.
- orders: placeOrder(requestId, customerId, lines), getOrder(orderId).

orders.placeOrder is a saga implemented in orders only, following the 8 steps in section 16.1 exactly:
- Order state machine persisted in the orders schema: PENDING, RESERVED, AUTHORIZED, CONFIRMED, REJECTED, FAILED.
- A module-local outbox table in the orders schema, written in the same transaction as each state change, and a scheduled relay that executes outbox entries by calling the target @RpcApi method (idempotent by requestId): the compensations (inventory.release, payments.void) and notifications.send. The relay retries with backoff, and a notifications outage never fails or delays the order.
- Same requestId sent twice returns the same order and causes no duplicate reservation, authorization or shipment.
- No cross-module transaction, no event, no direct database access across modules.

Seed data (loaded only in the "demo" profile from demo-only Flyway locations inside each module): a handful of products with base prices; customers cust-standard, cust-gold (tier discount) and cust-declined (payment method that is declined); stock levels; plus special SKUs sku-oos (no stock) and sku-undeliverable (shipping always fails).

Demo fault hooks (demo profile only, in each module that needs one): notifications can be toggled down, payments can be told to decline, inventory can be given extra latency; controlled in-process through a small FaultControl bean that stage 6 exposes over HTTP.

Tests:
- Module slice tests per module (@ApplicationModuleTest) mocking collaborators' -api.
- Saga tests in orders with mocked APIs for every scenario in section 16.5: happy path, gold discount, out of stock, payment declined (release called), shipping failure (void and release called), notifications down (order still CONFIRMED, notification delivered after recovery), idempotent retry.
- Contract tests per -api, run against every binding from stage 3 for the interdependent chain orders -> shipping -> inventory -> catalog, proving identical results and exception types.
- app-modulith integration test: real PostgreSQL (Testcontainers), all eight modules, the full scenario table from section 16.5.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes.
- With app-modulith running locally, a raw JSON-RPC call to orders.placeOrder for each scenario in section 16.5 gives the expected outcome (give me the curl commands).
- The dependency graph in your report matches the mermaid graph in section 16.1 exactly.

docs.title: Stage 6: Assembly apps and the local demonstration harness
docs.text:
Stage 6: finalise the app artifacts and build the local demo harness for the eight-module domain (section 16 of the design). Everything runs on localhost; Docker is used only for PostgreSQL.

Apps and baked configuration:
- app-modulith: all eight impls; application.yml sets every module enabled with binding local and rpc.server.enabled=false. Startup validation rejects any remote or loopback-* binding.
- app-macro: all eight impls; no module wiring baked in; everything comes from profiles and environment variables. Profiles: monolith, front, fulfilment, accounts (the groupings in section 16.2), one profile per single module (orders, catalog, pricing, inventory, customers, payments, shipping, notifications), loopback-codec, loopback-http, and the database layouts needed by split-dbs.
- Per-service apps app-<module>-service for all eight modules, generated by scripts/new-service-app.sh from one template so they stay uniform. Each contains its own -impl plus exactly the -api artifacts of the modules it calls (its allowedDependencies), module enabled, rpc.server.enabled=true, every other module remote with a required URL. Add a Maven enforcer rule that fails the build if a service app's -api dependencies differ from its module's allowedDependencies.
- Ports and databases as in section 16.3 of the design (8080 all-in-one; 8081-8083 groups; 8081-8088 one per module; PostgreSQL on 5432, 5433, 5434).

Demo aids (enabled only in the "demo" profile, which implies "dev"):
- GET /demo/topology: for each module in the process, enabled or not, binding (local, loopback-codec, loopback-http, remote), target URL, datasource host/port and schema (never the password).
- Call trace with correlation: a boundary interceptor on every @RpcApi call from one module to another records correlation id, caller, callee, method, binding actually used, depth, duration and outcome in a bounded in-memory buffer. The correlation id is generated at orders.placeOrder (or taken from a request header), propagated in-process and in an HTTP header on remote calls. GET /demo/trace?correlationId=... returns the records of that process. Log one line per call, such as "pricing -> catalog.getProduct [local] 1 ms ok". Keep it minimal; stage 8 extends the interceptor.
- POST /demo/faults to toggle the fault hooks from stage 5 (notifications down, payments decline, inventory latency); it affects only modules enabled in that process.
- Startup banner listing the topology.

Scripts (bash, in scripts/):
- scripts/db.sh up|down: starts/stops the three Postgres containers with docker-compose.demo.yml and runs docs/db/bootstrap.sql for all eight modules (schemas, migration role, runtime role).
- scripts/demo.sh <mode> up|down|status, where mode is one of: modulith, macro-modulith, groups, microservices, microservices-macro, loopback-codec, loopback-http, split-dbs. It starts the right JVMs with the right profiles and ports, writes PID files and logs under .demo/, waits for readiness, and prints the topology URLs. "down" stops everything it started.
- scripts/smoke.sh: runs every scenario in section 16.5 against whichever process hosts orders, checks outcomes and exception types, and prints the merged call tree for one order. Exits non-zero on any difference from the expected results.
- scripts/trace.sh <correlationId>: queries /demo/trace on every running demo process and prints one merged call tree, with the binding shown on each edge.
- scripts/demo-all.sh: runs every mode in turn (up, smoke, down) and prints a summary table of mode, processes, bindings seen (from the traces), and pass/fail.

Out of scope for this stage: image publishing, CI pipelines, service-to-service security, cloud configuration. A Dockerfile per app is optional; do not spend time on it unless asked.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes.
- `scripts/demo-all.sh` passes for all eight modes from a clean checkout with only Docker and a JDK installed. The summary table shows the expected bindings: local for modulith and macro-modulith; mixed local and remote exactly as the edge table in section 16.2 for groups and split-dbs; all remote for microservices and microservices-macro; loopback-* for the loopback modes.
- scripts/trace.sh prints the same call tree shape for one order in every mode, differing only in the binding on each edge.

docs.title: Stage 7: API documentation (OpenAPI and OpenRPC)
docs.text:
Stage 7: generated API documentation from the @RpcApi interfaces.

- Generate an OpenRPC document and an OpenAPI 3.1 document at runtime from the @RpcApi interfaces using reflection, with record schemas produced by swagger-core's model converters. First verify which swagger-core/springdoc versions support Jackson 3 and Boot 4; if none do, generate the schemas ourselves from the records and tell me.
- OpenAPI: one operation per method at POST /rpc/{module}/{method} (the alias path from stage 3), operationId = "<module>.<method>", descriptions from optional @Schema/@Operation annotations on the API interfaces.
- Endpoints: /rpc/{module}/openapi.json and /rpc/{module}/openrpc.json per module, plus a merged document at /rpc/openapi.json for deployments that run several modules. Served only when rpc.server.enabled=true.
- A Maven goal or test that writes the generated documents from the compiled -api artifacts to target/ so CI can publish them; nothing generated is committed.
- Serve Swagger UI only in the dev profile.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes; tests assert that adding a method or field to an @RpcApi interface changes the generated documents, and that a document is valid against the OpenAPI 3.1 schema.
- I can open Swagger UI in dev and call inventory.getStock through the alias path.

docs.title: Stage 8: Hardening and compatibility checks
docs.text:
Stage 8: parity, compatibility and failure behaviour.

- Boundary interceptor: an AOP interceptor around local cross-module calls (the @RpcApi beans injected into other modules) that adds Micrometer metrics and tracing identical to remote calls, and, behind a property (modules.boundary.suspend-transactions, default true), suspends any active transaction for the call (PROPAGATION_NOT_SUPPORTED semantics) so local behaviour matches remote behaviour. Tests prove an outer transaction is not joined.
- API compatibility check: a build step (japicmp or equivalent) comparing each -api artifact with its last released version and failing on removed or changed methods, renamed fields, or removed exception types; additive changes pass. Document how to set the baseline version.
- Failure behaviour tests for the client proxy: timeout, connection refused, server returns a JSON-RPC error, malformed response, and a retry on an idempotent method. Each maps to the documented exception type.
- Extend the stage 6 call trace interceptor with the metrics and tracing described above, and add failure tests for the stage 5 saga and outbox: kill the callee mid-call, return a malformed response, restart the relay, and confirm no duplicate side effects (idempotent requestId) across the whole domain.
- Update docs/design/macro-service.md where the implementation differs from it, and list every deviation in your report.

Definition of done:
- `mvn -q verify` passes.
- Every deviation from the design document is either removed or recorded in the document, and I have approved it.

docs.title: Stage 9: Final verification and handover
docs.text:
Stage 9: final verification.

- Run the full reactor build, all contract tests, all four bindings, and the `scripts/demo-all.sh` covering every demo mode (modulith, macro-modulith, groups, microservices, microservices-macro, loopback-codec, loopback-http, split-dbs). Report the results in a table.
- Re-run ApplicationModules.of(Application.class).verify() in app-modulith and attach the module canvas/component diagrams generated by Documenter to docs/generated (CI-generated, not committed).
- Write docs/README-dev.md: how to run each shape locally, how to add a new module (api/impl layout, stereotypes, migrations, datasource config, startup validation, adding it to a grouping, generating its per-service app), how to change an @RpcApi interface safely, and how to add a new deployable service app.
- List any open risks or follow-ups, including anything that depends on library versions that may change.

Definition of done:
- Everything above is committed with the message "stage 9: ..." and the final report lists exact commands for each shape.

docs.title: Result cache: @Cached
docs.text:
Many of the 17 to 20 calls inside one order are reads of data that rarely changes: the same customer looked up five times, the same product looked up by two modules. @Cached lets a read method opt in to having its result reused for a short time.

@RpcApi("customers")
public interface CustomersApi {

    @Idempotent
    @Cached                                   // 30 seconds, 10,000 argument lists, per process
    Customer getCustomer(String customerId);
}

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
graph LR
  Caller --> Cache["@Cached layer<br/>(Caffeine, per method)"]
  Cache -- miss --> Bean["the bean the caller would get:<br/>local impl or remote proxy"]
  Cache -- hit --> Caller
  • A Caffeine cache per annotated method, keyed by the argument list, with a time-to-live (ttlSeconds, default 30) and a size bound (maxSize, default 10,000).
  • It sits in front of every @RpcApi bean: local implementations as well as loopback and remote proxies. A hit costs about the same (a few microseconds) wherever the module runs, so callers behave the same in every mode.
  • Failures and null results are never cached. A customer that does not exist yet is looked up again next time.
  • When the RPC dispatcher serves a remote caller, the layer is skipped for that one call (the remote caller has its own cache); calls the implementation makes while serving it do use their own caches.
  • In the call trace a hit appears as binding cache, so latency tables show hits separately from real calls.

docs.title: What is annotated
docs.text:
Method Why it is safe customers.getCustomer, customers.getPaymentMethod slowly changing reference data catalog.getProduct, catalog.productExists slowly changing reference data

Deliberately not annotated: inventory.getStock and getReservation (they change constantly), every method that changes state, and pricing.quote / shipping.quote (derived values, a possible later candidate).

docs.title: Switching it off
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh groups start --cache off                    # or: rpc.cache.enabled=false (env RPC_CACHE_ENABLED=false)
scripts/perf.sh --modes groups --cache both                 # measure with it off and on

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
Staleness

A change to a customer's tier or payment method is invisible to callers until the entry expires. Keep the time-to-live short, and annotate only data where that is acceptable.

Per-process caches

Each process has its own cache. With several instances of a service they can briefly disagree, and in the eight-process modes each service warms its own cache (hit rates are lower there; see the measurements).

Results are shared

The same object is handed to every caller, so result types must be immutable (the demo's are records).

Where it lives: platform/rpc-api (Cached, CacheSignals), platform/rpc-spring-boot-starter (CachingBeanPostProcessor); it is on main.

docs.title: Follow-up delivery: outbox or Spring Modulith events
docs.text:
After an order changes state, orders still has to tell other modules something: release a reservation, void a payment, confirm to the customer. These are follow-ups. They cannot be done atomically with the database commit (they are calls to another module), and they must not be lost.

The pattern

  1. In the same transaction as the order change, store a record that says "this follow-up must happen".
  2. After the commit, deliver it by calling the other module through its @RpcApi.
  3. If delivery fails, retry until it succeeds. Delivery is at-least-once, so the targets are idempotent (keyed by request id).

Because delivery goes through @RpcApi, it works in every mode. A notifications outage never fails the order.

docs.title: Two implementations, one switch
docs.text:
modules.orders.async picks the mechanism (OrderStore publishes through a small FollowUps port):

outbox (default) events Record a row in the module's outbox table a Spring Modulith event in orders.event_publication Delivery OutboxRelay polls the table and calls the target an asynchronous listener runs right after the commit Retry exponential backoff, 30 attempts, built in exponential backoff and maximum attempts supplied by OrderEventRedelivery (the registry has none) Code we own the relay, repository, entity, signal (about 340 lines) a repository adapter, the redelivery policy, a stand-in bean (about 440 lines) Delivery speed 20 rows per second (one batch of 20 per one-second poll) immediately Idle cost none (scans only when woken, with a slow idle scan) none (scans only after a failure, shortly after start, and on a slow idle scan) 
scripts/demo.sh modulith start --async events         # or: modules.orders.async=events (env MODULES_ORDERS_ASYNC=events)
scripts/perf.sh --modes modulith,groups --async both

An unknown value fails at start-up with a clear message. Both tables always exist; only the selected mechanism's components are created.

docs.title: What it took to fit Spring Modulith's registry to one-schema-per-module
docs.text:
Spring Modulith's event publication registry is the library version of the outbox. Fitting it to a design where every module has its own pool, transaction manager and database roles needed adapting:

  • The registry's own methods are @Transactional without naming a manager, and there are eight. ordersTm is @Primary. That works only because orders is the one module that publishes events.
  • Modulith's JDBC repository is package-private, wants a single DataSource and opens a connection at start-up. Module pools must not connect at start-up, so OrdersEventPublicationRepository implements the same table and statements over the orders pool.
  • @ApplicationModuleListener includes @Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW), which cannot name a manager and would hold an orders connection during the remote call; the listeners use @Async + @TransactionalEventListener instead.
  • Every process that contains the orders jar gets Modulith's event auto-configuration, which refuses to start without a repository; a stand-in bean covers processes that do not host orders.
  • Retry timing is not part of the library.

The full list, with the reasoning, is in the spike write-up.

docs.title: Which is better?
docs.text:
On the request path they are indistinguishable. The difference is how fast the follow-ups drain under load, which is measured here: events deliver immediately, the outbox at the speed of its relay. That speed is a tuning limit of this relay (a larger batch would close most of the gap), not a limit of the pattern.

Beyond speed, the two behave differently under load:

  • The outbox can be tuned and copes well with bursts. Follow-ups wait in a table and the relay drains them at its own pace (batch size, poll interval), so a burst of orders is absorbed and delivered afterwards, and the work is spread over time instead of competing with the requests.
  • Events run entirely inside the JVM. Delivery happens on the application's own executor, so the follow-up work grows with the order rate and loads the same JVM that is serving the orders. They deliver immediately when there is headroom, but they give no way to smooth a burst other than sizing the process.

Where it lives: modules/orders/orders-impl (FollowUps, OutboxFollowUps, EventFollowUps, OutboxRelay, OrderEventRedelivery); all of it is on main.

docs.title: Parallel quotes
docs.text:
At the start of orders.placeOrder three calls are independent reads: check that the customer exists, price the lines, price the delivery. Run one after the other, their latencies add up. Run together, the wait is the slowest of the three.

gantt
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat %s
    section Sequential
    customers.getCustomer :a1, 0, 1
    pricing.quote         :a2, 1, 5
    shipping.quote        :a3, 5, 11
    section Parallel
    customers.getCustomer :b1, 0, 1
    pricing.quote         :b2, 0, 4
    shipping.quote        :b3, 0, 6

(Illustrative durations in milliseconds.)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Parallel.Pending<Customer>      known   = Parallel.supply(() -> customers.getCustomer(customerId));
Parallel.Pending<Quote>         priced  = Parallel.supply(() -> pricing.quote(customerId, quoteLines));
Parallel.Pending<ShippingQuote> shipped = Parallel.supply(() -> shipping.quote(customerId, shipLines));
known.join();                        // joined in the order a sequential run would have thrown
Quote quote = priced.join();
ShippingQuote delivery = shipped.join();
  • Each call runs on its own virtual thread.
  • join() rethrows the failure unwrapped, and the joins happen in program order, so a caller sees the same exception it would have seen before.
  • Thread-bound context is carried into the worker: the logging MDC (correlation id, trace id) and the demo call-trace depth, through registered propagators. Anything else thread-bound that matters to a call (a security context, a transaction) must be registered too, or not used inside a parallel call.
  • It is for reads only. Calls that change state keep their explicit order, because the saga's compensation logic depends on it.

docs.title: Switching it off
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh microservices start --parallel off      # or: modules.orders.parallel-quotes=false (env MODULES_ORDERS_PARALLEL_QUOTES=false)
scripts/perf.sh --modes microservices --parallel both

The sequential code is still there when it is off.

docs.title: Expectations
docs.text:
It removes waiting, not work, so it helps where calls are slow (a network hop) and does little where they are free (an in-process call). The measurements show exactly that. It does not make the machine do less: at saturation the gain shrinks.

Where it lives: platform/rpc-api (Parallel), OrdersService; it is on main.

docs.title: The eight deployment modes
docs.text:
The same modules, the same API interfaces and the same tests run in eight shapes (the glossary defines each term and separates the ones that sound alike). Only the artifact that is started and its configuration change. scripts/demo.sh <mode> start brings up PostgreSQL in a clean state and starts the mode.

Mode Processes Artifact Cross-module calls Databases modulith 1 app-modulith all local one instance, eight schemas macro-modulith 1 app-macro, profile monolith all local one instance, eight schemas loopback-codec 1 app-macro, profile loopback-codec all through the JSON codec, in memory one instance, eight schemas loopback-http 1 app-macro, profile loopback-http all over HTTP to itself one instance, eight schemas groups 3 app-macro, profiles front, fulfilment, accounts local inside a group, remote between groups one instance, eight schemas split-dbs 3 as groups as groups three instances (A, B, C), one per group microservices 8 eight app-<module>-service jars all remote one instance, eight schemas (a schema, roles and pool per service) microservices-macro 8 app-macro eight times, profile = module all remote one instance, eight schemas (a schema, roles and pool per service)

All of them serve the orders entry point and the demo shop on port 9181, so a client or a load test is pointed at the same URL in every mode.

Shared or split databases

The Databases column is each mode's default (--dbs shared: one instance, a schema per module). scripts/demo.sh <mode> start --dbs split gives every deployable unit its own PostgreSQL instance, so the database layout follows the deployment: groups uses 3 instances (one per group), microservices and microservices-macro 8 (one per service, ports 5432 to 5439), and a one-process mode stays on one. No code changes: it only sets each module's datasource URL. split-dbs is the name of groups --dbs split. The eight-instance layout starts eight PostgreSQL containers, so it needs the memory for them.

docs.title: Picking one
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  Q1{"Need independent<br/>scaling or deployment<br/>of parts?"}
  Q1 -- no --> Q2{"Want to prove the<br/>boundaries hold?"}
  Q2 -- no --> A["modulith"]
  Q2 -- yes --> B["loopback-codec / loopback-http<br/>(every call crosses the API boundary)"]
  Q1 -- yes --> Q3{"How many<br/>deployable units?"}
  Q3 -- few --> C["groups / split-dbs"]
  Q3 -- many --> D["microservices"]
You want to know... Use The cheapest possible shape, no boundary overhead modulith Whether the code still works when every call is serialised (no shared objects, no shared transactions) loopback-codec What a real HTTP hop costs without a second process loopback-http The middle ground: a few deployable units, local calls inside each groups Whether a group can move to its own database server split-dbs The full microservice shape, one jar per service microservices The same shape built from the single macro jar microservices-macro

The same checks run in every mode

scripts/smoke.sh runs seven scenarios (happy path, tier discount, out of stock, payment declined, shipping failure, a dependency being down, an idempotent retry) against whichever mode is running and asserts the results, the exception types and the binding on every edge. scripts/demo-all.sh runs it against all eight on a clean database.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Item Port Orders entry point and shop (every mode) 9181 groups, split-dbs 9181 front, 9182 fulfilment, 9183 accounts microservices, microservices-macro 9181 orders, 9182 catalog, 9183 pricing, 9184 inventory, 9185 customers, 9186 payments, 9187 shipping, 9188 notifications PostgreSQL 5432 (A), 5433 (B), 5434 (C; B and C only in split-dbs)

What each shape costs is measured in the performance section.

docs.title: Modes that run in one process
docs.text: Four shapes, one JVM. They differ in how the module boundary is crossed, which makes them a clean way to price each layer: a method call, a serialisation, an HTTP request.

docs.title: modulith
docs.text:
graph LR
  subgraph "one JVM (app-modulith) :9181"
    O[orders] --> P[pricing]
    O --> S[shipping]
    O --> I[inventory]
    O --> Y[payments]
    O --> N[notifications]
    O --> C[customers]
    P --> K[catalog]
  end
  PG[("PostgreSQL A<br/>8 schemas")]
  O -.-> PG
  • Run: scripts/demo.sh modulith start
  • What it is: the fixed all-in-one assembly. app-modulith refuses to start if any module is disabled or bound to anything but local.
  • Calls: direct method calls through the @RpcApi interface; no serialisation.
  • Databases: eight schemas on one PostgreSQL instance, each with its own roles and its own connection pool.
  • Use it for: the lowest-cost baseline, and day-to-day development.

docs.title: macro-modulith
docs.text:
• Run: scripts/demo.sh macro-modulith start
  • What it is: the configurable jar (app-macro) with the monolith profile, which enables every module as local. Every mode of this app is built from modules, so there is no genuine monolith here: this mode is a modulith (every deployment has all modules enabled) built from the configurable jar. The profile is still called monolith.
  • Why it exists: it proves that the macro jar, which can become any other shape, behaves the same as the fixed assembly when it is configured as a monolith. Its numbers should match modulith; they do (see the measurements).

docs.title: loopback-codec
docs.text:
graph LR
  O[orders] -->|"encode → JSON-RPC → decode"| D[RpcDispatcher]
  D --> P[pricing impl]
  • Run: scripts/demo.sh loopback-codec start
  • What it is: every cross-module call is turned into a JSON-RPC request, dispatched in memory and the answer decoded, but never leaves the JVM.
  • Why it exists: it finds the bugs that a local call hides: code that relies on shared mutable objects, on classes that do not serialise, or on a transaction that the callee silently joined. If a scenario works here, no object identity or shared transaction is being smuggled across a boundary.
  • Not allowed in production: the registrar rejects loopback bindings under a prod/production profile.

docs.title: loopback-http
docs.text:
• Run: scripts/demo.sh loopback-http start
  • What it is: every cross-module call is a real HTTP request to 127.0.0.1:9181, served by the same process.
  • Why it exists: it isolates the cost and behaviour of HTTP (connection handling, timeouts, error mapping, retries of @Idempotent methods) from the cost of a second process. It is the nearest thing to a microservice shape that still starts in one JVM.
  • Watch for: the process calls itself, so the HTTP server threads are shared between the entry point and the callbacks.

The cache applies in every binding

The @Cached layer sits in front of local, loopback and remote beans alike, so a cache hit costs about the same in all four. See the cache.

  • What it is: groups --dbs split, with each group on its own PostgreSQL instance: front on A (5432), fulfilment on B (5433), accounts on C (5434).

(Orders' edges, plus pricing → catalog as an example; every other edge is also a remote call.)

  • Run: scripts/demo.sh microservices start
  • Database: one PostgreSQL instance (port 5432) with a schema per module. Each service has its own schema, roles and connection pool, but they share the one database server.
  • What it is: eight separate jars, app-<module>-service, generated from one template (scripts/new-service-app.sh). Each contains only its own implementation plus the -api artifacts of the modules it calls, which an enforcer rule checks.
  • Why it exists: it is the conventional microservice shape, so every comparison has an honest reference point.
  • Cost: eight JVMs, and every call that the cache does not answer (about 14 of the 20 per order, with the cache on) is a network hop.

docs.title: microservices-macro
docs.text:
• Run: scripts/demo.sh microservices-macro start
  • Database: the same as microservices: one PostgreSQL instance with a schema per module; each process uses only its own module's schema, roles and pool.
  • What it is: the same eight-process shape, but built from the single macro jar run eight times, with the profile named after the module that process hosts.
  • Why it exists: one artifact to build, test and ship, deployed as eight services, which is the central claim of the project. Its measurements match microservices, which shows the single artifact costs nothing extra at runtime.

Resource use

The eight-process modes start eight JVMs with -Xmx2g each by default, so up to 16 GB of heap. On a laptop, microservices and microservices-macro are the heavy ones; set DEMO_JAVA_OPTS (for example -Xmx320m) to shrink them.

How the split shapes compare under load is in the measurements.

docs.title: Performance: what each shape costs
docs.text: All eight deployment modes run the same code and the same tests. This section measures what the different shapes cost, and what three optional features win back. Everything is measured on one machine with a deterministic, skewed workload (method).

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
• The boundary is cheap. The network is not.

    In one process, going through the API costs nothing measurable. Serialising every call costs 2% of the throughput, an HTTP hop to yourself 30%, three processes 44%, eight services 64%.

  • One artifact, no penalty.

    The configurable macro jar performs like the dedicated assemblies: macro-modulith is within 1% of modulith, microservices-macro within noise of microservices, and split-dbs equals groups.

  • Cost is per call.

    A call costs about 0.5 ms in process, 0.9 ms over HTTP to yourself and 1.5 to 2.2 ms between processes, and an order makes about 20 of them.

  • Two features win a good part back.

    A result cache adds 5 to 18% throughput in the split modes (3 to 5% in one process). Running three independent reads in parallel adds 4 to 16% in the modes where calls are remote, and nothing in a single process.

docs.title: How to read this, and what to take from it
docs.text:
Finding Evidence Splitting costs roughly 1 to 1.7 ms per call between processes, on one machine. With about 20 calls per order that is most of the difference in time per order between one process and eight services. per-call latency Group the chatty parts. groups keeps 40% of the calls that reach a module local and is about 55% faster than eight services (247 against 159 orders/s). modes Use the cache for reference data, and parallel reads where hops are real. Both are off-switches, so they can be measured on your own workload. cache, parallel quotes, every combination The follow-up mechanism does not affect the request path, but it decides how fast background work drains. Outbox and events perform alike on an order; the outbox delivered about 20 notifications a second, events delivered immediately. delivery speed

Treat the absolute figures with care

One machine, 2 GB JVMs (see JVM settings for how that default was chosen), cheap calls and loopback networking with no TLS, authentication or proxies. Compare the shapes with each other; do not quote 445 orders per second as a capacity. A real network, TLS and any gateway or mesh make the split shapes cost more than shown. The method page lists what the measurements do and do not say.

docs.title: JVM settings: bigger heaps, C2 and parallel GC
docs.text:
The demo's default JVM is now -Xmx2g -XX:+UseParallelGC with the full JIT; this page shows how that default was chosen. It repeats the mode comparison on the 128 GB, 32-CPU test machine with 16 concurrent clients, with the earlier small JVMs (-Xmx320m, C1-only JIT, serial GC) and with larger ones, to see how much of the result is the JVM settings rather than the architecture. These runs were made before the VACUUM ANALYZE step was added to the measurements, so their absolute numbers are a few percent different from the headline numbers.

Short answer. Giving each JVM more memory changes nothing measurable (1 GB and 2 GB agree, over five repetitions each); letting the JIT use C2 does most of the work, and the parallel collector adds a little throughput and a clearly better 99th percentile. Together they make the in-process shapes 37 to 61% faster. They leave the shapes that cross a process boundary almost where they were. The ordering of the shapes is unchanged, but the gap between the monolith and eight services widens from about 2.0x to 2.8x.

  • Heap size makes no measurable difference. 1 GB and 2 GB agree within the noise for every mode and collector, so 1 GB is enough for these JVMs at this load.
  • The collector barely moves throughput. Parallel is ahead of serial by 0 to 8%, most visibly on the in-process modes (modulith 437 against 470 at 1 GB). Medians are identical.
  • The collector shows in the tail. The 99th percentile is lower with the parallel collector in almost every row, for example 52 against 144 ms for modulith at 1 GB and 167 against 198 ms for microservices at 2 GB. docs.title: What to take from it
docs.text:
• In-process shapes gain the most. modulith, macro-modulith and loopback-codec rise from about 305 to 440 orders/s (cache off) and from about 330 to 465 (cache on). Their p99 also tightens, from about 160 ms to about 55 ms in most cases, which suggests the C1 runs' tails were compilation and collection pauses.
  • Process boundaries dominate once the JVM is fast. microservices and microservices-macro stay at about 140 (cache off) and 165 to 175 orders/s (cache on) under both settings: each order still pays about 20 calls over HTTP, and the code on either side of them was not the bottleneck.
  • The cost of splitting looks larger, not smaller. With C1, microservices ran at 50% of modulith; with C2 it runs at 36%. A faster JVM speeds up the work between the calls, so the calls become a bigger share.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One run per configuration, so differences below about 5 to 8% are noise.
  • The first comparison changes the JIT and the collector together; the repeated matrix varies only heap and collector, and C2 is inferred as the remainder.
  • Still one machine, loopback only, and a shared PostgreSQL server; see the method page.
  • The other pages use the 2 GB parallel-GC default and the VACUUM ANALYZE step, so their absolute numbers differ slightly from the C2 figures here.

What it shows

  • In one process the two are within noise (450 against 433 orders/s, outbox against events).
  • Events were 2 to 7% lower in throughput in seven of the eight modes (macro-modulith shows +1%, which is noise) and the median order 0 to 7% higher. The cause was not investigated (the registry's extra status updates and the asynchronous executor are candidates). It is a small cost, close to the run-to-run noise. Events run inside the same JVM as the orders, so the cost can be expected to grow with the order rate; the outbox moves that work to a table and a relay that can be tuned.

docs.title: Delivery speed
docs.text:
The request path cannot show this, because follow-ups are delivered after the order returns. This test is older than the 16-client runs: it used the former small demo JVMs, ran before the VACUUM ANALYZE step and is not part of scripts/perf.sh, but the result is a property of the relay, not of the machine. The test: place 978 orders flat out, then time how long until every confirmation message has actually arrived in the notifications module.

Time until every notification is deliveredseconds after the last order was placed; smaller is better0.010.020.030.040.050.0outbox: lag 48.9 soutboxlag: 48.9 s48.9events: lag 0.1 seventslag: 0.1 s0.1Show the numberslag (s)outbox48.9events0.1 Delivery Orders placed Time to place them Notifications delivered Last one arrived after outbox 978 3.4 s 978 of 978 48.9 s events 978 3.5 s 978 of 978 0.1 s
  • Events delivered every message 0.1 s after the last order.
  • The outbox needed 48.9 s, about 20 messages a second. That is the relay's design: it claims one batch of 20 entries per one-second poll. It is a tuning limit of this relay, not of the pattern: a bigger batch or a shorter poll interval (modules.orders.outbox.poll-interval) would close most of the gap.
  • Under sustained load the outbox backlog keeps growing while orders arrive faster than 20 a second, so a notification can be minutes late, though the order itself is never slowed.

Note also how each behaves as the order rate rises. The outbox can be tuned and handles bursty load well: follow-ups queue in a table and drain at the relay's pace, so a burst is spread over time. Events are all in process, so their work grows with the order rate and loads the same JVM that serves the orders. This test measures neither effect directly; it only times a drain after a flat-out run.

Which to choose is a judgement, not a benchmark: events drain faster out of the box and come with a library's semantics, at the cost of an adapter and a retry policy to maintain; the outbox is simple, self-contained and can be tuned.

docs.title: What the combinations show
docs.text:
• The mode decides, the switches adjust. In every combination the order of the modes is the same: modulith, macro-modulith and loopback-codec together at the top, then loopback-http, then groups and split-dbs, then the two eight-service modes at the bottom. No setting of any switch changes that.
  • The effects roughly multiply. In microservices the cache is worth +18% and parallel quotes +15%; with both off the throughput is 116 orders/s against 161 with both on, +39%, which is about the product of the two. Switching events on costs a further 3 to 7%, so the worst combination is 112 orders/s against 161 for the best (30% lower) in microservices, against 387 and 450 (14% lower) in modulith.
  • The switches matter most where calls are most expensive. The worst combination is 14 to 16% below the best in the one-process modes, 22% below in loopback-http, 13% below in groups and 30 to 31% below with eight services.
  • Outbox against events is a small cost. Events were behind the outbox in 40 of the 44 pairs of cells, by 4% at the median, within a range of 7% behind to 5% ahead.
  • Splitting the databases changes nothing measurable. Shared against split is within noise in all three modes that have the choice (the comparison), and in every combination of the other switches.

The raw reports of the 88 runs are in the raw reports.

docs.title: Method
docs.text: How the numbers on these pages are produced, and how far to trust them.

docs.title: The machine
docs.text:
Everything runs on one machine: 32 CPUs, Linux 6.12, JDK 25, PostgreSQL 17 in Docker, the load generator and all application processes together. Each JVM runs with -Xmx2g -XX:+UseParallelGC (the default of demo.sh; override it with DEMO_JAVA_OPTS), which is up to 16 GB of heap for the eight-process modes. JVM settings shows how that default was chosen.

What a single machine means

A hop between processes here is a loopback TCP connection on one host, typically 1 to 3 ms. There is no TLS or mTLS, no authentication on each call, no load balancer, gateway or service mesh, no service discovery, no real network latency or loss, and no cross-zone traffic. A real deployment has most of these, so the cost of splitting shown here is a lower bound for its network and security part. Client and servers also compete for the same CPUs, which flattens differences once the machine is busy.

docs.title: The workload
docs.text:
scripts/perf.sh drives orders.placeOrder with the realistic profile:

Aspect Value Customers 10,000, popularity skewed (Zipf, exponent 0.8) so a few customers order often Products 2,000, popularity skewed (Zipf, exponent 1.0) Lines per order 1 to 4 (mean 2.0), 1 to 3 units per line Customer mix 8% gold tier, 2% whose payment is always declined Order stream deterministic for a given seed, whatever the thread timing

Skew matters more than size: real traffic reuses a few customers and products, and that reuse is what a cache can exploit. Declined orders are an expected business outcome; they are counted and shown separately, and excluded from the latency figures.

docs.title: The load
docs.text:
• Closed loop: each of N concurrent clients sends its next order as soon as the previous one returns. N is 16 for every run on these pages.
  • Persistent connections, so connection set-up is not part of the measured round trip.
  • Warm-up: 200 orders, not measured, so JIT compilation and connection pools are settled and the cache has seen its popular keys. After the warm-up (and a short settle for its asynchronous work) the driver runs VACUUM ANALYZE on every PostgreSQL instance in use, so the measured run starts with fresh planner statistics and no dead rows from the seed and the warm-up.
  • Measured run: 1,500 orders.
  • Clean database every run: demo.sh start wipes and re-initialises PostgreSQL, the driver bulk-loads the customers, products and stock, and every start is from the same state.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
Two layers, from the same run:

  1. Client round trip of each placeOrder: orders per second, and min, mean, p50, p90, p95, p99 and max in milliseconds.
  2. Every module-to-module call inside those orders. Each process records the calls it makes (caller, callee, method, the binding that was actually used, duration). The driver reads them back per order and reports count, mean and percentiles per call and per binding. About 20 calls happen inside one order on average (17 for a one-line order), so a single run yields tens of thousands of call samples.

A call served by the result cache is recorded as its own binding, cache, so hits are visible and are not mistaken for fast network calls.

docs.title: What it does not tell you
docs.text:
Read the figures with these in mind

  • One run per configuration, except the headline table (5 runs per mode). Run-to-run noise on this machine is about 3 to 5% for throughput and p50. Differences smaller than that are noise; p99 and max are noisier still (single outliers of 50 to 100 ms appear in otherwise identical runs).
  • Call tracing has a cost. Recording each call adds a little overhead to every configuration equally. --no-trace measures round trips only.
  • It is a demo domain. Calls are cheap (one primary-key query each), so the network and framework share of the time is larger than it would be for services doing real work.
  • No real network and nothing in the path: loopback only, no TLS, no authentication, no proxies or mesh. No real data volume, and no failures during the measurement.

docs.title: Reproducing it
docs.text:
scripts/perf.sh --modes all --cache both --orders 1500 --warmup 200 --concurrency 16         # the mode comparison
scripts/perf.sh --modes <mode> --cache both --parallel both --async both --dbs both ...      # every combination of the switches, once per mode
scripts/perf.sh --modes all --cache on ...                                                   # repeated 5 times for the headline means

Each run writes a timestamped markdown report with the modes side by side, plus the raw samples, to .demo/perf/<timestamp>/. The tables and charts on these pages are generated from those saved summaries by scripts/perf_site.py (modes, cache, parallel, follow-ups) and scripts/jvm_report.py (the headline means and the JVM study), never typed by hand. The prose around them quotes their numbers by hand, so re-read it when you regenerate.

docs.title: In one process, the module boundary is almost free
docs.text:
• modulith and macro-modulith are the same thing built two ways, and they measure the same (445 and 442 orders/s).
  • loopback-codec forces every call through JSON encoding and decoding, in memory: 98% of the throughput, median 35.2 ms against 34.2 ms. Serialisation is a small tax, and it is the price of proving that no object identity or shared transaction crosses a boundary.
  • loopback-http makes every call a real HTTP request to the same process: 70% of the throughput and a median of 48.1 ms. The cost of the protocol, without a second JVM, is already 30% of the throughput.

docs.title: Between processes, the price is paid per call
docs.text:
• Three processes (groups): 56% of the throughput, median 62.2 ms. Calls inside a group stay local at about 0.4 ms, calls between groups cost about 1.5 ms.
  • Eight services (microservices): 36%, median 96.9 ms, and every call is remote at about 2.2 ms.
  • split-dbs equals groups (250 against 247 orders/s): putting each group on its own PostgreSQL instance cost nothing measurable here. (On one machine the database servers do not compete for the same network link; across real hosts it would.)
  • microservices-macro, the same eight processes built from the single macro jar, matches microservices (156 against 159, inside the run-to-run noise). The one-artifact claim costs nothing at runtime.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:
If you value... Pick The best latency and throughput modulith (or macro-modulith, equal) A boundary that is proven to hold, at 2% cost loopback-codec as a test configuration A few deployable units with most of the speed groups: more than half of the monolith's throughput with three processes instead of eight Independent deployment and scaling of every module microservices or microservices-macro, at about a third of the throughput on this machine

groups is the interesting middle: it keeps the chatty chains (pricing → catalog, shipping → inventory → catalog) inside one process, so those calls stay at local cost.

docs.title: Wire formats: gzip and BSON over HTTP
docs.text:
Does compressing the JSON-RPC envelope, or sending it as BSON, make calls between processes cheaper? Tested on this project's HTTP calls only. Local calls and the in-memory loopback-codec binding never use these formats, because there is no network to save and nothing to compress for.

Short answer. Keep plain JSON as the default. gzip shrinks big envelopes a lot (to 17 to 31% of their size between groups at 40 to 150 order lines) but only shows a latency benefit on constrained links, never on loopback, and it does little for the small envelopes of normal orders. BSON is larger than JSON for these messages in every case measured.

What these measurements can and cannot show

Everything ran on one machine over loopback, with no TLS and no bandwidth limit, so a smaller message cannot arrive any sooner. The end-to-end runs therefore show the cost of the formats (and bytes saved), never a latency win. Where compression could win is worked out separately, from a CPU benchmark and the bytes saved (break-even). One run per configuration, so differences below about 5 to 8% are noise.

docs.title: What was built
docs.text:
• rpc.client.wire (demo.sh --wire, perf.sh --wire) chooses how the HTTP transport encodes the envelope: json (default), gzip, bson or bson-gzip.
  • The /rpc/{module} endpoint accepts all four and answers in the format the caller asks for (Accept, Accept-Encoding); plain JSON callers are unchanged.
  • The BSON conversion is checked against the MongoDB library itself (the tests build and read BSON with it), so it is real BSON.
  • Each process counts the envelope bytes it sends and receives, before and after encoding, so the runs report bytes on the wire per order, not estimates.

A default that would have corrupted the baseline

Spring 7's JDK HTTP client has compression on by default: it adds Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate to every request and silently decompresses the reply. The platform's transport had been sending that header all along, harmlessly, since no server compressed. Once a server honours it, the "plain JSON" baseline would have been compressed too, and the real compressed sizes would have been invisible. The transport now turns that off and chooses the encoding itself.

docs.title: Bytes on the wire
docs.text:
Per order, from the counters of every process. "JSON bytes/call" is the average call (its request and response envelopes together); the last three columns are the share of the JSON bytes that crossed the wire.

Order size Mode HTTP calls/order JSON bytes/order JSON bytes/call gzip bson bson-gzip 1 to 4 lines (the realistic mix) loopback-http 13.7 4,340 318 89% 107% 98% 1 to 4 lines (the realistic mix) groups 8.0 2,911 364 85% 107% 94% 1 to 4 lines (the realistic mix) microservices 14.3 4,533 316 89% 107% 98% 40 lines loopback-http 55.3 21,075 381 63% 112% 71% 40 lines groups 8.3 11,013 1327 31% 116% 39% 40 lines microservices 56.1 21,300 380 63% 112% 71% 150 lines groups 8.6 34,521 4029 17% 119% 24% 150 lines microservices 168.0 68,833 410 57% 114% 64%
  • At realistic order sizes (1 to 4 lines, envelopes of about 150 to 200 bytes) gzip saves 11 to 15%, BSON adds 7%, BSON+gzip saves 2 to 6%. Too little data per call for gzip to find much to remove.
  • Big envelopes compress very well. Between groups the calls that carry the order lines average 1.3 KB at 40 lines and 4 KB at 150 lines, and gzip takes them to 31% and 17%.
  • microservices and loopback-http compress less (63% at 40 lines, 57% at 150 lines for microservices). There most of the calls are tiny per-line lookups (a product, a stock level) of about 400 bytes whatever the order size, and only a few carry the lines.
  • BSON is larger than JSON at every size (107 to 119%). Field names are kept, every value gets a type tag and every string a length, and arrays carry index keys; JSON's digits and brackets are already compact.

docs.title: What each format costs in CPU
docs.text:
Measured with no network, database or web server in the way: encode an object tree to bytes on the sender and decode it on the receiver, for envelopes shaped like the demo's order calls (a request carrying n order lines). Median of warmed batches, microseconds per envelope.

Order lines JSON bytes Format Bytes vs JSON Encode µs Decode µs Extra µs vs JSON Break-even link speed 1 133 json 133 100% 0.2 0.4 0.0 - 1 133 gzip 131 98% 2.9 2.1 4.4 0.5 MB/s (4 Mbit/s) 1 133 bson 152 114% 0.4 0.4 0.2 never (no bytes saved) 1 133 bson+gzip 143 108% 3.1 2.1 4.7 never (no bytes saved) 4 235 json 235 100% 0.3 0.5 0.0 - 4 235 gzip 150 64% 3.2 2.3 4.7 18.1 MB/s (145 Mbit/s) 4 235 bson 278 118% 0.6 0.5 0.3 never (no bytes saved) 4 235 bson+gzip 176 75% 3.8 2.5 5.4 10.8 MB/s (86 Mbit/s) 10 439 json 439 100% 0.6 0.8 0.0 - 10 439 gzip 172 39% 3.6 2.8 5.0 53.1 MB/s (425 Mbit/s) 10 439 bson 530 121% 1.0 1.0 0.5 never (no bytes saved) 10 439 bson+gzip 209 48% 4.4 3.1 6.1 37.6 MB/s (301 Mbit/s) 40 1,459 json 1,459 100% 1.8 2.6 0.0 - 40 1,459 gzip 264 18% 6.6 4.9 7.1 168.8 MB/s (1,350 Mbit/s) 40 1,459 bson 1,820 125% 3.0 3.3 1.9 never (no bytes saved) 40 1,459 bson+gzip 385 26% 8.8 5.8 10.2 105.2 MB/s (842 Mbit/s) 150 5,220 json 5,220 100% 6.6 10.3 0.0 - 150 5,220 gzip 591 11% 17.2 14.0 14.3 323.6 MB/s (2,589 Mbit/s) 150 5,220 bson 6,621 127% 10.8 11.8 5.7 never (no bytes saved) 150 5,220 bson+gzip 1,006 19% 25.1 16.2 24.4 172.5 MB/s (1,380 Mbit/s)
  • gzip adds 4 to 14 µs per envelope (more for bigger ones). BSON as a codec costs about the same as JSON text (0.2 to 5.7 µs more) but produces larger output, so there is nothing to recover.
  • The platform's transport currently passes JSON text between the proxy and the wire, so a BSON call there also pays a text parse and print that a native BSON path would skip. That extra cost is not in this table.
  • gzip is the plain GZIPOutputStream per call (a new compressor each time, default level, no dictionary). Reusing compressors, or a dictionary trained on the envelopes, could make small messages compress better and cost less. Not tried.

docs.title: Where compression pays
docs.text:
Compression helps when sending the bytes it saves would take longer than compressing and decompressing them. The break-even column is bytes saved ÷ extra CPU, in MB/s: below that link speed gzip wins, above it JSON is faster. Read with the bytes columns above:

Envelope Break-even link speed What it means about 130 bytes (1 line) 0.5 MB/s (4 Mbit/s) only a very slow link; gzip saves 2% about 235 bytes (4 lines) 18 MB/s (145 Mbit/s) slow or shared links only about 440 bytes (10 lines) 53 MB/s (425 Mbit/s) helps below roughly 400 Mbit/s, not on gigabit about 1.5 KB (40 lines) 169 MB/s (1.35 Gbit/s) helps on 1 GbE, loses on 10 GbE about 5 KB (150 lines) 324 MB/s (2.6 Gbit/s) helps on 1 GbE, loses on 10 GbE
  • Small envelopes never justify compression for latency on a datacentre network. Large ones do on gigabit and slower links, and not on 10 GbE.
  • This is the latency case, for calls made one after the other. Bytes also have a cost of their own (cross-zone or egress charges, shared links, TLS work per byte), which is not measured here and favours compression.
  • BSON never saves bytes, so it has no break-even.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
1. Default stays json. The normal order calls are about 150 to 200 bytes, where gzip saves about 12% and BSON costs 7% more.
  2. If you enable compression, do it by size. Compress envelopes above roughly 1 KB, where it pays on gigabit links, and leave the small ones alone. A minimum-size threshold is not implemented yet (it is the obvious next step; the setting would be per client).
  3. Do not use BSON for JSON-RPC envelopes of this shape. It is larger, slightly slower, and its advantages (binary values, exact typed numbers, partial reads) are not used here.
  4. Measure on the real network. The case for compression depends on bandwidth, TLS, cost per byte and payload sizes that this one-machine demo does not have. The tooling to do it is perf.sh --wire all, with --lines N for larger orders.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• perf.sh --modes loopback-http,groups,microservices --wire all --async events ..., four clients, result cache and parallel quotes on. Events delivery so each run's follow-ups drain at once; the wire format is independent of that choice.
  • Order sizes: the realistic mix (1 to 4 lines, 1,200 orders), --lines 40 (500 orders) and --lines 150 (250 orders). More lines mean more calls too (about 134 and 464 module calls per order).
  • The CPU table: WireCostBenchmark (a test that only runs with -Dwire.bench=true).
  • Raw reports: realistic orders, 40 lines, 150 lines.
  • Limits: loopback, no TLS, one run per configuration, JSON text between the proxy and the transport, a new compressor per call.

docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.

docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.

  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.

  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.

docs.title: Performance run 20261027T181004Z
docs.text:
• Started: 2026-10-27T18:10:04+00:00
  • Commit: c0a5e07
  • Host: 32 CPUs, Linux 6.12.113+deb13-amd64, Python 3.13.5

docs.text:
• A cache is only as good as the key reuse inside its TTL: compare hit rates across profiles, and across run lengths.
  • Tracing adds overhead; compare with --no-trace for pure client round trips.
  • Client and servers share one machine, so CPU contention is part of every figure.
